Releases

What changed in each version of Xenon, newest first. The app updates itself; every release and its checksums are also on GitHub.

Versions

5.0.010 November 20264.11.1316 October 20264.11.129 October 20264.11.112 October 20264.11.1026 September 20264.11.920 September 20264.11.811 September 20264.11.75 September 20264.11.628 August 20264.11.522 August 20264.11.410 August 20264.11.36 August 2026

5.0.0 10 November 2026

Added

  • Your copy's number

    A widget bought with Sparks now knows which copy it is, numbered in the order people bought it, so a numbered edition can show "No. 042" on your screen. The number stays yours on every PC you install it on and through every update. A Sparks sale with an end date now also ends by itself on that date: nobody new is charged after it, and a copy already bought keeps opening. For creators: init.edition in the Widget SDK, and Your copy's number in Xenon Maker.

  • Choose what a Store widget shows

    A widget can now list its own choices (which readings to show, a smaller shape, when to appear), and Xenon draws them in that widget's card under Widgets in the Xenon menu, in your language. The same choices are under Store → Installed → Options on every screen, so a widget used as a dashboard tile, in a browser, on a paired phone, a Mac or Linux can be changed too, and Back to the widget's choices puts them back as the widget set them. They are kept across restarts and updates, and Bit can tell you which widgets have choices and change them when you ask, wherever the widget is. A widget made to sit over a game can also size its own box to what it shows, so a small counter takes only the room of its numbers instead of a slice of the screen; for those widgets the menu hides the size and the "merge into tabs" rows, and they are never offered as a tab of another widget. A widget's own choices have their own tab on its screen, What it shows. For widget makers: manifest options and fit, see the Widget SDK guide.

  • Which program slows your game down

    When a game stutters or runs slowly because the processor is busy or the memory is full, Xenon now names the program, other than the game and the system, that uses the most of it, and how much: "browser is holding 3.3 GB of memory". The Game performance tile shows it after the reason, the answer to the Why does it stutter? key says it, and Bit tells you when you ask. Widgets get it too, in the perf stream. It works on Windows, macOS and Linux, reads the list of programs only while there is something to explain, and names a program only when it uses enough to matter.

  • How much energy your PC used, in kWh

    With the sensor history on, Xenon now adds up what your PC draws, hour by hour for the last 3 days and day by day for the last 90. Ask Bit "how much did my PC use this month?" and it answers in kWh, and works out the cost if you tell it your price per kWh. Widgets can show it too, with the new energy permission. A widget that puts today's kWh next to the clock keeps it counting even when the widget itself is on no page. When your power supply reports its own draw the figure is the whole PC; otherwise it is the CPU and graphics card only, and Xenon says so. Hours when the PC was off are never counted.

  • Tell Xenon an app is not a game

    Game mode starts when an app fills a screen, so a maximised app could be taken for a game. Settings → Performance now has a Not games list: add the app in front with one tap, or remove one you added. Game mode and everything that waits for a game then leave that app alone. The Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps are never taken for games. A Deck key, a widget button and Bit ("this is not a game") can do it too.

  • Keys for game mode, Performance Mode and the sensor history

    New Deck actions switch game mode, turn Performance Mode on or off, rule out the app in front as not a game, and turn the sensor history on or off or change how often it records. Widgets can use them too, once you allow them, and the same actions are in Xenon Maker and in Bit.

  • Choose how often the sensor history records

    Settings → Performance → Sensor history now takes a reading every 1, 2, 5, 10 or 15 minutes (5 as before). A shorter interval catches short spikes in temperature or load. The History tab has a new 6 hours range that shows every reading at that interval, before the hourly and daily ones.

  • Tap a notification to open its app

    In the Notifications widget, tapping a notification brings its app to the front, or starts it if it is closed, and the pop-up of a new notification has an Open button. It works on Windows and Linux for apps installed on the PC; a notification from a web page brings the browser forward when it is open. From a paired phone or tablet the tap does nothing, since the app would open on the PC. A Deck key and Bit can do it too.

  • A page for what is new in 5.0

    xenon-app.com/5 shows each new thing on its own sheet, with a short clip or picture and a Bit of its own: Liquid Glass, widgets on your main screen and when they show, game performance, capture and Instant Replay, Bit, Xenon Maker and supporters, then the smaller changes and the downloads. It is in all seven languages of the site, every clip has a key to pause it, and with reduced motion nothing moves.

  • Your widgets in your recordings, when you want them

    In the Xenon app on Windows and macOS, the Capture section of the Xenon menu has Widgets in captures. Turn it on and the widgets on your screen, the performance readings too, show in screenshots, videos, Instant Replay and the apps you stream or record with. It stays off unless you turn it on, so a capture shows only your screen, and the menu and pop-ups never show. On macOS 15 and later another app that records the screen may still show them; Xenon's own captures never do. On Linux no capture tool can leave a window out, so the menu says the widgets always show there. You can also ask Bit: "show my widgets in my recordings".

  • Any widget can be glass, in one tap

    Widget style now opens on Material: Theme, Liquid Glass, Clear, Frosted, Solid or No panel, each a real sample over the wallpaper, with the colour of the glass below them. It works under every look, not only Liquid Glass, and the numbers are still there under Fine tune. When the glass cannot show, on a plain background or with blur off on a low-power graphics chip, the window says so and takes you to the setting. You can also ask Bit: "make the music widget purple glass".

  • A new Ambient scene

    The built-in scene is now one big clock made of glass, with the colours of your wallpaper running through the numbers, and up to three quiet cards for weather, music and what comes next. It fills an Edge strip, a monitor, a tablet and a phone, and with only the clock on it grows to fill the screen. The cards are real glass now: before, they blurred nothing. Nothing moves on its own any more, so a screen left on all evening stays still and costs less. On an OLED panel the whole scene walks a few pixels once a minute so the clock does not mark it. On a 12-hour clock AM and PM stay off the screen, as on a phone, and screen readers still hear them. The greeting line, the event counter and the coloured dots are gone. The same scene is the desktop wallpaper and the screensaver.

  • The island, the top bar and the side handles are one glass

    On the Liquid Glass look they now share one material with a soft lit edge, so the colours of your wallpaper come through them. The full top bar is no longer a panel across the screen: it is three glass groups on one line, which leaves the tiles about 60 pixels more, and its clock reads on one line like the island. Bit's mark stands by itself without the green plate, the handle on each side is a slim grabber, and the phone's bottom bar has plain keys with larger words. The green "online" dot and the dot for a single page are gone: only a problem shows a mark now. A look you chose in Settings stays as it is.

  • Calmer widgets on the new look

    On Liquid Glass a widget is now one sheet: its cards lose their outlines, keys are a soft fill, and a chosen tab is a neutral thumb, so colour is left to what the widget is telling you. System graphs share one colour, tags lost their pill shape, and the Timer goes big when it is alone. A look you chose in Settings stays exactly as it was.

  • Widgets read properly on the light theme

    Today in the calendar, fan speeds, Vitals numbers, the power supply, Wave Link sliders and the YouTube and Twitch lists were drawn for a dark sheet. They now have the contrast they need, and a widget without its panel gets a light edge behind dark words instead of a smear.

  • Music with nothing playing

    The hint wraps instead of being cut, and the picture no longer carries a "No artwork" caption.

  • A new Weather widget

    It opens with the temperature and one plain line about what changes next, like "Rain from 10:00 PM" or "Dry for the next 7 hours". Under it the coming hours are a single line with the chance of rain beside each hour, then the days with bars in the colours of their real temperatures, then the details that matter. A warning such as bad air comes first. The painted sky is gone, and rows that do not fit leave whole instead of being cut. Everything you turned off in Settings stays off, and the one-line version is still there.

  • One question for every widget: when do you see it?

    Open a widget in the Xenon menu and pick Always, On the desktop, In game or On an app. That one choice sets where it goes and when it shows, and Other situations has the rest. The list is split by those answers, and every row says if the widget is showing now and, if not, what brings it.

  • A map of your real screens

    The Widgets section draws your monitors as they stand on your desk, with the widgets on them. Drag one anywhere, even to another monitor, and where you let go is where it stays. The buttons on top show what appears in a game, on your apps or on the desktop.

  • Moving a widget is simpler

    On the map and on the screen a drag follows your finger up to the very edge, pulls to the edges, the middles and the sides of other widgets with a line you can see, and never changes the size. Tap a widget on the screen and you get its choices in words: when, size, tabs, remove.

  • Resize a widget by its corner

    The picked widget on the map and on the screen has a corner to pull. The performance readings grow as a whole, so their letters stay readable, and dragging them no longer turns them into a strip across the screen. They now stop exactly where you let them go, anywhere on the screen, with the dashed frame centred around them and no black bar behind them or behind the edit bar.

  • A widget's screen you understand at a glance

    The picture of your screens stays still on one side while you choose, and the choices sit in four tabs beside it: When, Where, What it shows and Look. When opens first, with five pictures to tap: Always, On the desktop, In game, On an app and At certain moments, which opens the situations (music, a call, going live and the rest). Where holds the screen, the corner and the page, Look holds the size, how see-through it is, the background, and Take off the screen. The tab you left stays open when you come back to that widget. More options is gone. On a phone the tabs sit under the picture and stay at the top while you scroll.

  • Pause, play, next and previous reach your player even when Windows' media list is stuck

    The buttons used to report success while nothing happened. Xenon now tells the app that is playing directly, also when it is closed to the tray. A browser tab cannot be reached this way: it comes back when the Windows service does.

  • A paused song stays on screen

    With a stuck media list a pause used to read as nothing playing, and the widget set to show when there is music vanished with its Play button. It now stays for 5 minutes after a pause, whatever the player, and comes back within about 3 seconds when the music starts again.

  • Lyrics show when Xenon only hears the song

    The message about a playback with no duration was wrong for a normal song: Xenon now finds the words by title and artist and shows them as plain text.

  • A widget held up by the menu lets go when you minimize the menu
  • The menu waits for you while you move widgets

    After Move with the mouse, pressing Done brings the menu back where you left it, so you can go on and close it yourself.

  • Removing the last widget while you move widgets no longer leaves a blank window

    Pressing Remove on the last widget on your screen left a white window titled Xenon where the menu was, with move mode still on. The same window could also appear after a few minutes of moving widgets. Now move mode ends by itself, the menu comes back, and no white window is left. The widget you remove also no longer jumps to the left before it goes.

  • You see the widget you are changing

    While a widget's screen is open in the menu, the widget stays on the real screen even if its rule hides it right now, for example one set to show only in a game. It goes back to its rule as soon as you leave.

  • Paired access no longer locks you out after a slow start

    With phones allowed, a PC that started slowly could end with Xenon running but unreachable until it was restarted. It now reopens by itself.

  • FPS, Benchmark and "Why does it stutter" now read the right numbers when widgets sit above a game

    With a widget over a borderless game the frame rate could read 8 instead of 240, Benchmark stopped as too short, and normal play looked like stutter. Xenon now counts every frame of that game.

  • A game in exclusive full screen keeps its keyboard

    The Xenon menu, Bit, the Store, Settings, moving widgets, area captures, the colour picker, the ruler and drawing cannot show over such a game, and opening them took the game out of full screen and left the keyboard reaching nothing. They now stay closed and tell you why, with the fix: borderless or windowed in the game's display settings. Whole-screen captures, recording, Benchmark and frame readings work as before.

  • Benchmark no longer counts a game closing

    When a game quits during a run, its last second is left out of the numbers and the file. One long frame on the way out could turn a steady 240 FPS into a 1% low of 50.

  • Benchmark and "Why does it stutter" now answer during a game

    , and closing a screen opened from a Deck key brings you back to the game.

  • Switching mode from a Deck key leaves the game in front

    The dashboard used to take the focus from the game you were playing.

  • The Mixer key fills the Xenon window

    , instead of a small card in an empty window, and the sound of a web view is called Edge WebView2.

  • "Move widgets" and "Show widgets" say when there are none

    , instead of doing nothing.

  • No more false "widgets cannot show over this game" notice

    , and the real one now shows during a game.

  • "Mark this moment" and "Clips from marks" now answer during a game

    Marking showed nothing while you played, and making clips gave no sign at all. A very short timelapse no longer reads "in 0:00".

  • Sending a capture to your phone from a Deck key now says it worked

    , and where to find it. If a replay clip cannot be saved, the key says so in a sentence instead of a raw code.

  • Deck keys say what happened, in plain words

    A key that cannot run right now, like Save replay with no game open, now shows one calm line that says what to do, without a red error or a code. Do not disturb and Copy to a folder confirm what they did, even with alerts held back.

  • Recording a key is easier to leave

    Click the button again, click anywhere else or press Esc to stop. A combination Xenon cannot use no longer ends in an error: the button says which one to try and keeps listening. The key that changes page moved to the screen of a page.

  • Undo, one step at a time

    Undo in the menu, on the screen or with Ctrl+Z takes back the last change. Put it back still returns everything to how it was when you started.

  • Adding a widget finds a free spot

    It no longer lands on top of another one, and it starts as what suits it: the game readings in game, the player when music plays, the rest always. You can change it right after.

  • Votes you can trust in the Store

    After you have really used something from the Store, for three days and some hours on screen, a small card asks how many stars it gets: at most once a week, never during a game, and closing it means it never asks about that item again. You can also vote on its Store page, or tell Bit. One to three stars can add a short reason, which the creator sees only as totals. You get ten seconds to undo, then the vote is final: one per PC, and reinstalling gives no new one. The average shows from five votes. Votes from older Xenon versions stop working once this ships. Settings has a switch to stop the asks.

  • Try the new look on your own screen

    An update keeps the look you have. What's New now has a sheet for Liquid Glass with a key, Try it on my screen: your dashboard melts into the new look and stays usable, with a small card to keep it or put yours back in one tap. Your look is saved first, as a card in Settings → Appearance → Themes, and it stays there whatever you decide.

  • A new look for new installs: Liquid Glass

    A fresh Xenon now opens on real glass tiles over a new wallpaper, Dusk, with a small top bar and plain labels. Where glass cannot work, the tiles go nearly solid so the words stay easy to read: on your desktop as widgets, on a low-power graphics chip, and with transparency turned off in the system. If you already use Xenon, nothing changes: your look stays yours. Liquid Glass is a new card in Settings → Appearance → Themes, and the look Xenon had until now is the Classic card next to it. Dusk is also a new wallpaper in Settings → Background, light in light mode.

  • A new home page for the website

    It opens on the product in colour, with the widgets people ask for most, one word at a time, a search box that says if Xenon has what you want, and a Download section with one column per system.

  • The whole website has the new look

    The guides, Download, Releases, the catalog, the form to publish a widget and the creator guide all open on a sheet of colour, with the same menu and footer. The Download page now links the .deb and .rpm files directly. In the catalog the supporter packs sit on their own yellow sheet, phones get a shorter list, and every pack opens on its picture. The publish form is now fully translated into Korean, Japanese and Chinese and its screenshot slots work from the keyboard, the page that follows a submission takes the colour of its state, and the creator guide has the real publishing steps. Links to a section no longer end up under the header when a banner is showing.

  • Packs in the catalog open in a proper window

    The picture is larger and every thumbnail is in view, the price and the keys stay at the bottom, and Esc, Back and the keyboard all work. On phones the filters wrap instead of hiding off the edge.

  • Emails match the website

    Every Xenon email, and the free trial and unsubscribe pages, now open with the green sheet of the home page: the logo and the name of the message, the text on white paper, in light and dark. A mail about a single new drop no longer says its name twice.

  • Calmer banners on the website

    The cookie box is shorter, with Reject and Accept side by side at the same weight. A drop banner you have already seen no longer pushes the page down on every page, and a phone shows one offer at a time.

  • The website says what Xenon is today

    It opens with "Xenon, widgets for your PC on any screen" in all seven languages, and the guides open the same way, because Xenon is no longer only for a second screen. Every page has one main key, named for your system, and the bar's Download fills once you scroll past it. Under the keys on the home, the Microsoft Store, Mac and Linux, downloads, Discord and GitHub sit in one row of logos. The GitHub star is gone: GitHub is its symbol alone.

  • Links to the website look right

    Every page now shows a title, a line and a picture when you share it, titles fit a results page in all seven languages, and the French home is listed for search engines.

  • The catalog's supporter shelf is clearer

    Every paid pack has one key, Become a supporter, and a code you already hold is a plain link beside it. Paid packs now read in your language in all seven languages of the site, a date that has gone by no longer looks like a deadline, and a banner opens the pack in your language.

  • The FAQ answers what people ask today

    It now covers the free trial, anti-cheat, recording, Bit, the Stream Deck and making your own widget, with a new section on price, in all seven languages. It also says plainly what the app counts, how to turn it off and how to uninstall.

  • Three clear supporter plans

    The site now shows Monthly, A whole year (the price of ten months) and the Supporter pass, with the one-off month as a plain line under them. The free 7-day trial is offered wherever it really applies: the home, the catalog and each paid pack that it opens. Become a supporter now goes straight to the membership page, and the catalog's Newest order and New badge work again.

  • Smaller fixes on the website

    The carousel arrows stay put under the mouse, the menus and the sort list match the site and work from the keyboard, the demo has the new bar and cookie box, and the Discord and GitHub marks show the live number of members and downloads.

  • Xenon Maker matches the website

    It has the same paper, corners and green main button, and it opens on the violet sheet of the Create page. Its name now stays whole in the editor's bar on a laptop or tablet, where only "xenon" was left.

  • Xenon Maker is easier to find

    The Store, Themes, Background and the Deck profile menu now have a link to it, next to the ones in Ambient, Settings and the Xenon menu, and Bit can tell you about it and open it.

  • Widgets and pages that appear when you need them

    In the Xenon menu, open a widget and pick When it shows: always, only when, or except when, then tap one or more situations. A game, music and an app come first, and More shows the rest: a live on OBS, a recording, a call, an app open, a running timer, Do Not Disturb, the PC under load, the PC idle, low battery and the time of day with the days you choose. One is enough. A widget page can do the same: it comes forward when the situation starts and gives back the page you were on when it ends. You can also ask Bit, for example "show the music only while music plays". What this PC cannot read is not offered, and a line says why.

  • After an update, Xenon tells you what changed

    A major version opens What's New full screen: Bit walks through a coloured sheet for each big feature, with a button to try it. It comes back at every start until you close it. A patch or a minor shows a small card with what was fixed, once, and if you skipped versions they arrive as one list. If an update fails, a card says why. With widgets only on the main screen, the same cards appear at the top centre of the screen. An update that lands during a game, an Ambient scene or the lock screen waits and shows when you are back, however long that takes, and only a really new install skips What's New: someone who used Xenon only from a phone or inside iCUE still gets it. To see What's New again, open it from Now in the Xenon menu, ask Bit or click the version number at the bottom of Settings.

  • Widgets as small as a button

    A Store widget on your screen can now shrink to 48 px, so one button that turns the lights off or runs a Streamer.bot action can stay in a corner all the time. At that size its move and remove controls sit beside it, and Bit knows the size too ("make it a button"). Allow, pressed on a widget on the screen, is now remembered: it used to ask again every time the widget loaded.

  • Bit can run on a server you already use on this PC

    Settings → Bit has a new choice, Local server, for programs that offer an OpenAI-compatible API. Xenon looks for it on the usual ports, so if it is running you pick this choice and you are connected; otherwise type its address. Add a key only if it asks for one. Xenon connects to it and nothing else: it installs and starts nothing, and it only accepts an address on this PC. Bit uses Xenon's commands when the model and the server support tools and the server has at least 32K of context; otherwise it answers without them and tells you why.

  • A new install starts with Bit, and 30 Sparks to try it

    On a fresh install the Bit chat is a tile on the first page, where the Agenda was, and the Agenda moves to the tab next to Playback. Bit is already the AI, on its fastest model, and the first message you send can bring 30 trial Sparks: no email, no key. They last 7 days, work for Bit on its fastest model only, can't be spent in the Store and end if you save a supporter code. If you already use Xenon, your layout and your AI stay exactly as they are.

  • Pictures in the Add list

    In the Xenon menu every built-in widget now shows a real picture of itself, and widgets from the Store show their Store picture. The Add list of the on-screen edit mode shows the same pictures. A widget you made yourself shows the first letter of its name.

  • The Widgets section is simple now

    It shows the page on your screen, one row per widget, with its picture, one line that says where it sits and a switch to hide it. Tap a row and the widget gets its own screen: a drawing of your screen with the widget on it, where you tap a corner to move it, and next to it all its choices. On an app, the drawing is that app's window with its logo. Tap a page's name to change the page on your screen; the line under the names says so. Add a widget has a screen of its own, with filters by kind next to its search, and a page has one too, for its name and for when it shows. Esc and the controller's back button step back one screen. Widgets in tabs get a row each, and hiding one tab hides its whole box.

  • Screens by their name

    The Xenon menu calls your monitors by their model, for example DELL U2720Q, and marks the main one. Two identical monitors are told apart by size or by a number. A screen that reports no name shows a number and its size.

  • The webcam row says what it does

    In the menu's Capture section the webcam row now says it puts your face in the video you record, and once you pick a corner it says the circle appears in the recording, never on your screen.

  • Screenshot lets you choose what to take, and shows what it took

    The Screenshot tile in the Xenon menu now freezes the screen and lights the window under the pointer: click it to take that window, drag for an area, or press Enter for the whole screen on Windows. On macOS and Linux it uses the system's own selection. A second tile, Whole screen, still takes the picture at once. The notification after a screenshot now shows the picture, so you can see which window or screen it took. The default keys stay the same.

  • Notifications open at the top centre of the screen

    With widgets only on the main screen, a notification now opens from the top centre as one small island of glass that grows into the card, and several wait behind a "+N" counter, as they already do on the dashboard. What's New and Bit's messages open at the top centre too. While one of those cards or a call holds that place, notifications sit in the top right corner beside it, or in the bottom right corner on a narrow screen, so nothing covers anything. On Windows a notification you close now rolls up towards the top of the screen and is gone, with nothing left behind it.

  • Shorter names on the Game performance tile

    Readings now say CPU, GPU, Frame or Loss next to their value, so 60°C sits beside CPU instead of CPU temp and a row stays short. The full name is still in the list where you choose the readings, and on hover.

  • The Game performance overlay shows FPS, and goes in a row or a column

    Plain FPS is there next to the 1% and 0.1% lows, each with a short explanation, and in its row in the Widgets section you choose Column or Row. In a row the text keeps its size and wraps to a second line rather than running off the screen.

  • Make your own widget, from the menu

    The Widgets section now says you can build one with Bit, in code or in Xenon Maker (Beta), and a widget you take off the screen can be put back from the same list.

  • Keys ready for the main functions

    Screenshot (Ctrl+Shift+F12), record (Ctrl+Shift+F11) and screen area (Ctrl+Shift+F8) are set for you, only where the combination is free. Change them in the Keys section.

  • The light theme reads properly everywhere you work

    The Xenon menu, Settings, the Store, the gallery, the mixer and the macro editor are now real paper: switches that are off show their track, green text and icons are dark enough to read, and windows that stayed dark with unreadable titles are light like the rest.

  • Three choices sit side by side in Settings

    The third one no longer drops alone onto a second line, and a long label in your language grows the button instead of being cut.

  • The performance HUD no longer keeps an old reading

    If Xenon restarted during a game, the last FPS stayed on screen with nothing running. It now goes back to the idle view within a few seconds.

  • A short editor for macros

    New shortcut or macro in the Keys section opens one small page: a title, what it does, the shortcut. Everything else stays behind More options. A macro needs a shortcut to be saved, and a combination already in use is refused with the name of the key that holds it.

  • Widget pages, explained and easy to switch

    The Widgets section says what pages are for and starts the second one for you. Next page works from the menu, a key, a macro, the Deck and Bit. Tap a page to see it: a new widget goes on the page you are looking at, and a widget's screen has a Page row to move it to another page. A page's choice now reads When I pick it or By itself, when…

  • Pick the scene for each screen in the menu

    Look now shows your screens as they stand on the desk, and the picture stays put while you choose. Tap a screen and its choices sit beside it in two tabs, each saying what it is set to now: Ambient scene and Dashboard background on the dashboard's screen, Wallpaper and Screensaver on every other one. Scenes are a list, one per line with a tick on the one in use, and the screen you tapped plays the scene you point at before you pick it. The screensaver tab holds how long the PC waits too. You change only that screen: a scene, or your own wallpaper and no screensaver. An Ambient scene on the dashboard no longer reads as the scene of your other monitors. More scenes, at the end of every list, leads to the Store, Bit, Xenon Maker and the editor, and the theme sits under the screens. Bit can change one screen too ("put the Classic scene on screen 3"), and the Deck key still pauses or resumes the wallpaper on every screen. A scene from the Store used to show the Classic one with no reason given when community widgets were off: Allow now turns them on too, and says so first, and until then the menu and Settings, Ambient say the scene is waiting, with an Approve button. Under the Classic scene the menu now has its parts too: clock, weather, music and events, on or off with one tap.

  • For the screen, in the Store

    The Store gets a filter for small widgets meant to stay on the screen. It appears once the catalog has some.

  • The Batteries widget now sees mice and keyboards on a USB dongle

    Logitech devices on their receiver or cable show their charge and whether they are charging, with or without G HUB open. Razer devices work the same way, in Beta. Many other brands now work too, with none of their programs installed, in Beta: mice, keyboards and headsets from Akko, MonsGeek, SteelSeries, HyperX, Glorious, Corsair and others, Xbox controllers and PlayStation controllers. A device whose dongle has no protocol Xenon knows does not appear. On Linux any peripheral the system reports appears, whatever the brand (Beta), and on macOS so do Bluetooth mice and keyboards. Xenon only reads: it changes nothing on the device, and asks about every 5 minutes so a sleeping mouse is left alone. A mouse that has gone to sleep on its dongle cannot answer, so its last charge stays on screen for up to 12 hours instead of the device disappearing. Ask Bit too: "how's my mouse battery?"

  • Battery reading can be switched off, and cannot take Xenon down

    Reading a dongle means sending the device a question, so Settings now has a switch to stop that; Bluetooth and the rest keep working. Each read runs apart from Xenon: a device that crashes or hangs it costs one reading and is left alone for a day.

  • Dongle batteries on macOS and Linux

    macOS reads them too, in Beta, once you allow Input Monitoring. On Linux the Batteries widget gives you the one line to paste so Xenon can reach them. Both say so on the widget, even when other devices are already listed.

  • Bluetooth headphones show their charge

    Some connected headphones were left out of the Batteries widget even though Windows knew their level. They now appear while connected, and leave the list when you turn them off.

  • AirPods and Beats in the Batteries widget

    While they are connected to your PC, Xenon shows the earbuds and, when it is known, the case. Windows and Linux keep no level for them, so Xenon listens to what they broadcast; levels move in steps of 10. On macOS it asks the system instead, which also brings in the level of other Bluetooth headphones. On Linux, any Bluetooth device that reports its battery to the system now shows too. macOS and Linux are in Beta.

  • Put one device's charge in the top bar

    In Xenon Maker, a widget can now name a device ("PRO X 2") and show its charge, or the device closest to empty, in the mini slot, a badge or a bar button, with no tile on screen. Bit can build it too, in the Maker and in Xenon.

  • Bit asks when it is not sure

    If what you asked could go very different ways, or points at something Bit cannot see, it stops and asks before making anything: numbered answers with what each one means, your own words, or You decide. Tap one or press its number. A clear request is still done straight away, without questions.

  • Your own pictures go into what the AI assistant makes

    Attach a photo, a logo or a GIF in the chat and ask for a background, a Deck key, an Ambient scene or a widget with it: the assistant puts that picture inside, instead of only looking at it. A picture that is too big is made smaller first, and a GIF keeps moving.

  • Ask the AI assistant to change a widget you already have

    Days later, in a new chat, say what to change ("make the countdown blue", "remove the small text at the top") and the assistant opens that widget, changes only what you asked and updates it on its tile. It works on the widgets you made, with the assistant, in Xenon Maker or by hand; a widget from the Store or from a share code belongs to its author and is never changed, and the assistant offers to make a new one of your own instead.

  • Make the top bar your own, in every style

    Settings → Dynamic Island is now Settings → Top bar. Under Look, pick one of six ready-made looks (Theme, Glass, Solid, Floating, Plain, Compact), each shown as a small drawing of the bar, and the bar at the top of the screen changes as you pick. Customize opens the finer controls: background (the theme's, glass, solid or none) with its own colour, opacity and blur, border, shape, shadow, size, buttons with or without a background, when button labels show, which button is highlighted, the separators in the Minimal capsule and the spacing. Each button in the Bar buttons list now has an arrow that opens its own options: another icon from the Deck's icon set, your own label, whether its label shows, and its own text and background colours, with a reset for that button alone. Typing a label on a button that shows icons only turns its label on, so the word you typed is the word you see. The side rails of Minimal and None have their own section: switch either side off, place them at the top, middle or bottom of the screen edge, choose how they hide (slide, fade or at once), after how many seconds, and whether the small handle stays once they have hidden. The side that holds Settings or Layout always stays on screen, so you can never lose the way back to them: move them to the other side first. The clock can use a monospace or a thin font and stop blinking its colon, and Notifications lets you choose where alerts appear (out of the Minimal capsule as before, or a fixed corner of the screen), with a button to show a test. You can also change the bar without leaving the dashboard: in Layout mode, Customize bar in the Layout panel opens a side sheet with the looks, the buttons and the side rails, and the bar changes behind it as you pick. On a phone the bar keeps its compact size. Reset the whole bar puts the look back too. With nothing changed, the bar looks exactly as it did. A theme you save or share now carries the bar's style too (its look, not your buttons or side rails), and a theme made on an unchanged bar leaves yours alone. To pass on the whole bar, Export → Export top bar makes a code with its look, buttons, clock and side rails; importing one shows what it sets before anything changes. A package can include it too, and the Store can list bars. While Settings → Top bar is open, the Settings window moves below the bar and clear of the side rails, so the real bar stays in view and you see every change on it as you make it. On a phone the bar's buttons stay icons even when labels are set to show always, because they would cover the clock there. Widgets can now add a button of their own to the bar (it asks for permission first): it appears on the left side, or in the left rail in Minimal, and you move it, hide it, rename it and recolour it like any other button. Removing the widget removes its button.

  • Xenon opens on Bit, on your theme's background

    While the dashboard loads, after a restart or a reload, the screen used to show every tile empty for a moment (dashes, no artwork, no events). Now Bit recharges on your theme's background until your settings and the first readings arrive, says hello, and the dashboard fades in. It never stays longer than 6 seconds, even with Xenon's server still starting, and a tap closes it at once, without the hello. On a new device the first load uses Xenon's dark background, because your theme is not known yet. The desktop app opens on the same Bit while it waits for Xenon to start, and its setup messages are now shorter and plainer. To turn it off: Settings → Appearance → Bit while loading.

  • One loading mark everywhere: Bit thinking

    Every wait in Xenon now shows Bit thinking: a web page opening in the Browser tile, the Disk tile reading a drive, cleaning or asking the AI, an update installing, a feed refreshing, the Optimize button working. It replaces the different spinning rings, and Bit stays still when animations are paused, in a game or with reduced motion.

  • A real layout for vertical screens

    On a screen taller than it is wide (a Xeneon Edge or a monitor turned on its side, a tall tablet held upright) the dashboard now arranges the same tiles for that shape: each page fills the screen, top to bottom, with wide tiles across the full width and, where there is room, small ones side by side. Before, the landscape layout was stacked as it was, so tiles kept a height made for a short screen and the page stretched to three screens long. You can rearrange and resize tiles on a vertical screen as usual: the changes are kept for vertical screens only, and the landscape layout stays as it is. Until you move something, the vertical layout follows your landscape one, including new tiles and pages. Reset layout in edit mode puts the current page back to the automatic arrangement. The Tile layout option in Settings still lets you choose Single column or Grid on that device. Upright tablets shorter than 1200 pixels keep the two-column view that scrolls. The top bar fits the shape too: the buttons share the first row and the clock sits centred under them, instead of the buttons scattered around a clock off to one side. Reported on Reddit.

  • Your Home Assistant dashboard as a tile

    Settings → Smart Home has a new section, Home Assistant dashboard: pick one of your dashboards (or type the address of any page of your Home Assistant) and Add as a tile puts it on the current page, in a Browser tile with its toolbar hidden. Sign in inside the tile the first time. To hide the Home Assistant sidebar, turn on the option that always hides it in your Home Assistant profile. Suggested on Discord by Forlin.

  • Choose which sensor shows your CPU and GPU temperature and power

    If your monitoring app shows a different temperature than Xenon, Settings → Performance has a new section, Sensor sources: for CPU temperature, GPU temperature, CPU power and GPU power, pick any sensor of your PC from a list grouped by hardware, each with its live value, so you can match the one your other app shows. Automatic stays the default and says which sensor it is using. Your choice is used everywhere the reading appears (System tile, Deck keys, lighting, AI). If the chosen sensor disappears (new hardware), Xenon goes back to Automatic and tells you. Available on Windows and Linux; a Mac reports one temperature per chip, so there is nothing to choose there. Widgets can also read every temperature, fan, power and clock sensor of the PC with the new sensors stream, for example the liquid temperature of an AIO cooler or an NVMe drive; the SDK guide is updated. Asked on Discord.

  • Any Discord widget can take you to the chat

    Store widgets and the ones you make in the Maker can now have a Reply button on a DM or a mention: it opens that conversation in Discord on your PC, the same way the built-in widget does. Widgets can also show the faces of the people in a call, and they know when they run on a paired phone or tablet, so they can hide what only works on the PC.

  • Widget makers see what the sandbox blocks

    A web page turned into a widget often stays blank, because widgets cannot load scripts from other sites, run inline scripts or onclick attributes, call fetch() themselves or use localStorage. In the Store, on the Installed tab, a widget you made or imported from a folder now shows a short list of what it does that the sandbox refuses, with the site or file involved and what to use instead. Xenon checks the widget's files when you open the tab, and also notes what the browser actually blocked while the widget ran. Widgets from the Store are not checked. Nothing is relaxed: the list only explains. Reported on Discord by SWu.

  • Switch keys on the Deck

    In a key's What it does tab, pick Switch under Behaviour: the first tap runs the key's action and lights it, the next tap runs the new Tap when on action (for example a second hotkey that stops a recording) and turns it off. A switch with no action at all still turns on and off, so other keys can follow it. A switch that follows a real state, like the mic, shows that state instead of its own. Switches share their state across every screen showing the Deck, and start off after Xenon restarts.

  • More ways for a Deck key to answer a press

    Behaviour, in a key's What it does tab, has three new kinds of key besides Button and Switch. Momentary runs one action when your finger goes down and another when it lifts, and stays lit while you hold it, like push-to-talk. Repeat runs its action at once and then again and again while you hold the key, like a volume key, and you choose the wait before it repeats and how often. Cycle steps through two to eight states, each with its own action and its own label, icon and colour in Look: each tap runs the state the key is in and moves to the next, and small dots on the key show where it is. Every key can also have its own press and hold time (half a second until you change it) and double tap time, and a switch can turn itself off after a number of seconds, as long as the dashboard that turned it on stays open. Widgets whose keys run a widget action now learn how the key was pressed, so one action can tell a press from a release or a state of a cycle.

  • One Title for each face of a Deck key

    In Look, with On or a state of a cycle picked, the Title at the top of the editor is the title of that face, so a switch can read LIGHT OFF when off and LIGHT ON when on. Leave it empty to keep the off title. Before, the On title sat in a second box further down and the one at the top always changed the off face.

  • Xenon in your language, everywhere

    In Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Russian about 1,100 labels and hints across the app still showed in English: settings, the Deck editor, widgets, the Store and smart home. Dutch, Italian, Korean, Japanese and Chinese had a few hundred between them. They are all translated now, and a test keeps new ones from slipping through.

  • Keys that ask for a second tap

    Turn on Ask for a second tap within 3 seconds before running (under Confirm) for keys you do not want to press by mistake, like shutting down the PC or ending a stream. The first tap shows "Tap again" on the key for three seconds; only a second tap in that time runs it.

  • A Deck key can turn other keys on and off

    The new action Deck state (in the System group) sets, clears or flips a named state. Any key set to follow that state lights up with it, on every screen. Give several keys the same name with different values and they work as a group where only one is lit, like scene buttons.

  • Clearer on and off for the whole Deck

    Deck appearance has a new section, Lit keys, with two switches that apply to every key following a state: Ring on lit keys draws a coloured ring around a key while it is on, and Dim keys that are off fades it while it is off. Both are off by default, so your Deck looks the same until you turn them on. The preview in Deck appearance shows them on any page: when no key on it follows a state, two of its keys stand in, one on and one off, so you can see what each switch does before you save. A new Glass base joins the others: a clear body with light falling through it and the dashboard showing behind.

  • A Deck that matches your other tiles

    Deck appearance has a new Base, Theme: the Deck's body is drawn like every other tile on the dashboard, with the same colour, border, corners and shadow, and it changes when you change theme or tile opacity. In a tab group the Deck simply sits on the group's tile. A new switch, Use the theme colours, gives the theme's colour to keys that have no colour of their own, to the background behind the keys and to the music bar, and they follow the theme when it changes. Keys with their own colour or picture keep it. The Comic key style keeps its own drawn board. Asked on GitHub by halluci293.

  • Colours for each tab of a tab group

    When widgets share one tile as tabs, the widget style editor has a new Tabs section, shown only on those tiles: the background of the tab bar, and for every tab its own background and text when it is selected and when it is not. Pick only a background and the text turns light or dark to stay readable. The colours also apply while the Deck is the open tab, and a colour left on Theme keeps following the tile and the theme.

  • Things you can touch on an Ambient screen

    An Ambient scene is for looking at, and four elements can now also be touched, each with its own Controls option: music (previous, play or pause, next), tasks (tap one to tick it), the new Notifications element (tap to show a hidden one, tap again to clear it from the screen) and the new Volume element (down, up and mute, by the step you choose). Controls on music and tasks stay off until you turn them on, so your scenes look the same. A tap on a control works even when the screensaver came on by itself, and the screensaver stays; a tap anywhere else closes it as before.

  • Edit an Ambient scene right on the screen

    Settings → Ambient → My scenes has an Edit button next to Delete. It opens the scene full screen as it really looks: tap an element to select it, drag it to move it, drag a corner to resize it, and change its options in the side panel (on a phone, a panel at the bottom). Add any element or any widget you have installed, duplicate, bring forward or send back, delete, undo, then Save. Close asks for a second tap when there are unsaved changes. New scenes are still made in Xenon Maker or imported as a code; Edit changes the ones you have.

  • Ambient scenes can do much more

    Every element now has its own opacity, an entrance (fade, rise, drop, zoom, pop, slide) and a motion that repeats (float, breathe, pulse, sway, drift, spin, blink), with speed and delay, and can show only at certain hours or on certain days, for example a "Good night" from 21:00 to 07:00. A scene can have up to six pages that change by themselves, and each element can sit on one page or on all of them. Backgrounds take gradients with up to five colours, round gradients, a slow movement, or your own dashboard wallpaper, video included. The clock can be analog or stacked, with a blinking colon and a lighter or heavier weight; the date has more formats; the weather can show its icon; system stats can be bars or rings; text gets letter spacing, line height and a glow; pictures can be black and white with a chosen focus point; shapes add pill, ring and soft glow. Motion stops with reduced motion, in game mode, in power saving and while you edit. Scenes made before look exactly as they did. The SDK guide lists every new option.

  • A small helper for widget code, and a guide for converting a web page

    xenon-client.js (in the SDK examples) is a file you copy into your widget: it says hello to Xenon for you, and gives xenon.fetch(), xenon.store and xenon.on(), which wait their turn so requests are not refused for being too frequent. It grants nothing a widget could not already do. The SDK guide has a new section, "From a web page to a widget", with what to change for each thing a normal page does.

  • Xenon Maker: make things for Xenon without code

    Settings → Widgets & sharing → Create now links to Xenon Maker, an editor on the Xenon site for widgets, themes, animated backgrounds, Ambient scenes, pages, Deck profiles, icon packs, sound packs and packages, with a preview inside the demo dashboard. Anyone can try it; saving projects, installing and submitting to the catalog are for supporters. What it makes installs through the same Import as any shared code, and the catalog form opens with the code already filled in.

  • Set each fan, and each LED, of your Corsair lights on its own

    In the Lighting settings, a Corsair device (an iCUE LINK or Commander hub, an AIO, RAM, a keyboard) now shows its real parts: every fan as a ring of its own LEDs, the pump, the RAM sticks, the strips, and each lighting zone of a motherboard iCUE controls (Zone 1, Zone 2…, the same zones iCUE lists, ARGB headers included). Tap a part (Fan 1, Fan 2, Pump), a single LED, or drag across several, and give them a colour, an effect of their own (breathing, rainbow, wave, aurora, candle, CPU temperature, album cover) or hand them back to Xenon. A wave runs across the LEDs you picked, fan after fan. The rest of the device keeps looking as it did, and LEDs you never touched follow Xenon. Timer, notification and Deck flashes still light the whole device. Everything is kept after a restart. Fans and pumps Xenon cannot tell apart are shown as one part, and their LEDs can still be set one by one. A Deck key with Control a light device, the Lighting tile and widgets can switch a device back to these settings with the new mode My LED colours.

  • Xenon now drives the RGB of GIGABYTE and AORUS motherboards itself, fan by fan

    Many fans and strips plug into the ARGB headers of the motherboard, chained one after the other, and until now Xenon could only light each header as one block, through iCUE. In Settings → Lighting → Connections, turn on Motherboard: Xenon talks to the RGB controller of the board over USB, with nothing else to install. Close RGB Fusion or GIGABYTE Control Center and remove the motherboard from iCUE first: when two programs drive the same lights, the colours keep switching. Then, under Devices, the motherboard card shows each of its ARGB outputs as a row. Because ARGB lights cannot tell what is plugged in, each output asks one question once: press Count the LEDs, and press + until everything plugged into it lights up white. From then on the output shows one dot per LED: tap a LED, or drag across several, and give them a colour or an effect of their own, like the LEDs of a Corsair device. Fans chained one after the other can also be split into pieces, one per fan or strip, with Split into pieces (All the same does it in one step when they are identical). Fans on a splitter all show the same LEDs, so a colour given to one LED lights the same LED on each of them. Rename gives an output a name you recognise, such as Fans or Desk strip: the output lights up white while you type, and the name is what the Deck and widgets show instead of Output 1. Newer boards that report how many LEDs each output has fill this in for you. The card lists every output the RGB chip can drive, so a board with fewer connectors shows one or two that light nothing: choose Nothing connected on those. The lights built into the board itself (the I/O cover, the chipset accent and similar) appear under Motherboard lights, one dot per light, and follow Xenon too. The setup is kept after a restart and can be redone at any time. Xenon never asks the board to save anything: turning Motherboard off or closing Xenon gives the ARGB outputs back to the board's own effects. If every LED of a long chain would be bright white, Xenon dims that output to keep it under 5 A, so an output nobody has counted yet can look dimmer in full white until it is set up. GIGABYTE's manuals allow 2 to 5 A per ARGB output depending on the board, and Xenon cannot tell which board it is on: check yours before plugging a long chain into one output. Shutting down, restarting or putting the PC to sleep switches every light of the board off first, outputs and built-in lights alike, so nothing stays lit or flickers on a PC that is off; the colours come back when the PC wakes up or Xenon starts again. This works on Windows and, in Beta, on Linux, where it has run on a simulated controller and not yet on a real board. Linux keeps USB devices away from normal users, so the first time the card shows one line to paste in a terminal, then press Search again. There is no macOS version: Macs do not have this chip.

  • Colour one part of a light from the Deck

    A new Deck action, Colour one part, picks one fan, strip or pump from a list and sets its colour, or hands it back to Xenon. The rest of the device keeps the look it had. Widgets can do the same with the new lightPart action, and read the lights and their parts with the new lighting stream; the SDK guide is updated.

  • Try the supporter pass free for 7 days

    A supporter drop in the Store, the unlock box and the Lyrics tile now offer Try 7 days free: it opens a page where you enter your email, and a trial code arrives by email. Paste it like any supporter code and, for 7 days on this PC, it unlocks the supporter drops (themes, backgrounds, widgets, Ambient scenes) and Lyrics. New drops usually join after their first 30 days. Limited drops need their own code, and Sparks and Dev cleanup are not part of the trial. Each PC can have one trial, and the 7 days count from the first unlock. Two days before the end, Xenon reminds you once a day. When the trial ends, what it installed comes off, your tiles stay where they were and say what was there, and the theme you had before comes back. A card then shows the Store pictures of what you used, with one button to keep them (5 USD a month on Buy Me a Coffee), and I have a code and Not now as plain links. The trial page opens in your language when it is one of the website's seven (English, Italian, Spanish, French, Japanese, Korean, Chinese), and shows pictures of what the trial opens. Widgets and Ambient scenes you try are never saved on disk in readable form: they stay locked in a file only Xenon can open during the trial, and they stop loading the moment it ends. If you become a supporter with the same email, Xenon saves your supporter code by itself, and Put it back on each tile reinstalls what you tried, right where it was. Promotional emails come only if you tick that box on the trial page. The one-week Lyrics trial that started from the tile is replaced by this one; a Lyrics trial already running ends on its own date.

  • The AI assistant can make any kind of Xenon creation

    Ask it for a page of tiles, an Ambient scene, a top bar, an icon pack, a widget, an animated background, a full theme with its own light and dark colours, a bigger Deck profile with folders and a look of its own, or a package that holds several of them. It never applies anything by itself: what it makes opens in the Import window, where you see what it contains and choose whether to add it, as with a code someone shared with you. Before opening it, Xenon checks it against the same rules as any import and tells the assistant what would be left out, so it can fix it first. It also checks its own work before showing it to you: text that is hard to read on its colours, tiles or elements that overlap or run off the screen, text too small to read, keys that do nothing, and widgets that would not pass the Store review (permissions they never use, hidden code, animations that keep running when the tile is hidden). It works the same by voice: a new version replaces the window of the one before. Sound packs are the one thing it cannot make, because they are audio files.

  • Bit without a key of your own: Sparks

    Sparks are Xenon's credits: the ones you buy never expire, and every month of support includes some. In Settings → Bit, the new provider Bit runs the assistant on Claude, with no API key to create. Questions, commands and voice always run on Haiku, the fastest model, for less than one Spark an answer. For creations (widgets, themes, backgrounds, scenes, Decks) you pick the model, and Xenon switches to it by itself as soon as you ask for one: Haiku (a widget costs about 3 Sparks), Sonnet (balanced, about 80) or Opus (the most accurate, about 150), at the Normal level. Next to the model you choose how much it reasons before creating: Light reasons little and suits simple requests, Normal is the recommended balance, Thorough gives a more polished result for about twice the Sparks and the time. The creation arrives at every level. You can also ask the assistant to change them, by voice or in the chat ("use Opus", "think more"), and a creation asked in the same message already uses the new choice. They are also in reach from the chat: the name of the model sits at the top, next to your Sparks, and a tap opens both choices with what a widget costs, without going to Settings. Every month of support includes 300 Sparks, spent first, which reset at the start of each month and do not carry over; anyone can buy more in the Store, under Sparks (500 Sparks for 5 USD, 1,050 for 10 USD, 2,200 for 20 USD), and bought Sparks never expire, even after your support ends. Pay with the email of your supporter code (Settings shows it, partly hidden); with no code saved, or with another email, a Sparks code arrives by email. After you tap a pack, Xenon checks for the new Sparks every few seconds and tells you when they arrive, usually within a minute, and the count also refreshes when you come back to the dashboard or into the chat. If they have not arrived after five minutes, Settings says so and what to check. Your Sparks are shown in Settings, in the Store and above the chat, next to a small spark; tap it to buy more. If you are a supporter and your assistant has no key set up, Xenon switches to Sparks by itself, so it works from the first message; a provider you set up yourself is never replaced. Voice and transcription stay local and free, small helpers (the chat summary, search, lyrics translation) run on Haiku, and Bit's lines use Sparks only up to the daily limit you pick in Vitals. On Sparks, everything the assistant creates also goes through the design half of the Store review, so it fixes what looks generic before you see it. Your supporter code goes to the Xenon hub only to open a session; after that, only a short-lived session token travels.

  • Widgets can ask your AI

    A widget can now ask a question to the AI you chose for Bit and show the answer: Sparks if Bit runs on Sparks, otherwise your own key, Ollama or your Claude or ChatGPT plan. The widget never sees your key and never picks the provider. It asks for this permission when you install it, the AI sees only what the widget sends, and Settings → Bit → Widget questions sets how many questions each widget may ask a day (20, 50, 100 or 200, 50 to start). For widget makers: the new ai manifest field and xenon.ai() in xenon-client.js, see the Widget SDK guide.

  • Some Store items can be bought with Sparks

    An item can now show a price in Sparks (1 Spark is 1 US cent): some open for supporters or for Sparks, a few only for Sparks. In the Store, an item that supporters or Sparks open says or N Sparks next to the supporter mark, and one sold only for Sparks says Unlock for N Sparks. You buy in a window of its own, in the item's colours: its picture, the price in Sparks and in USD, how many Sparks you have and how many stay after, what you get, then a box you tick to say you want it now, which ends your right of withdrawal, and one button, Buy now: nothing is spent without the box. Short of Sparks, the window says how many you need and Buy Sparks takes the button's place. On an item supporters open too, the pass comes first, with Buy just this one under it. Bit waits on the sheet, and you install from the same window. An item you already bought goes straight to Install now: no price, no box, nothing spent. A bought item is yours on up to 3 PCs, with every update published for it; opening it again costs nothing. You do not need to be a supporter: the Sparks code (XC-...) that arrives by email with your first pack pays too, and it goes in Settings, in the same box as the supporter code. If you are a supporter, your pass pays, and an item your pass already opens costs no Sparks. If you later become a supporter, the Sparks on your Sparks code move onto your pass. With only a Sparks code, Bit can use your Sparks too. Limited editions are never part of the 7-day trial, and an item sold only for Sparks is not either.

  • Answer the assistant's questions with one tap

    When the assistant needs a detail before acting, on any topic, it now offers the likely answers as buttons under its question: tap one to reply, or type anything else. In voice it reads the same options out loud, so you can just say one. It asks only when the answer changes what it does, so questions do not add Sparks for nothing.

  • Widgets on your main screen, no second monitor needed

    In the Xenon app on Windows, ask Bit "put the weather on the desktop, top right" (or use the new Deck actions) and the widget appears on your screen. There are three places to put it. On the desktop, it sits under your windows, comes up when you show the desktop (Win+D), and steps aside while a maximized window fills that screen. Over everything, it stays on top. Next to an app, it follows that app's window and hides when the app is minimized or closed. Clicks next to a widget reach whatever is underneath, and clicking a widget does not take the focus from the window you were using. Widgets on the same screen share one window, to keep memory low. Almost every tile now loads a lighter page that carries only what it needs and keeps updating, so a window of widgets uses less than half the memory of the dashboard. That includes the Agenda and its tabs, the System tile with its tabs (System, Volume, Microphone, History; the speaker and microphone pickers open inside the tile), Volume, Microphone, Calendar, Tasks, Timer and Notes as tiles of their own, and the Deck, whose keys work there as on the dashboard (to change a key, edit it on the dashboard). Lighting is light too. The Bit chat, the Browser and Bit's vitals still load the whole dashboard. Widgets can also share one box as tabs, the way tiles are grouped on the dashboard: ask Bit "put the music as a tab under the weather". A tab you pick on the desktop stays for that window. To arrange them by hand, ask Bit "let me move my widgets" or press the new Edit the widgets on screen Deck key: drag a widget to move it (it lines up with the screen edges and the other widgets), drag its corner to resize it, drop it on another widget to make them tabs, press Add to pick a widget that appears in the middle of that screen, and use the cross to take it off the screen or, on a tab, out of its box. The pin next to the cross lists the apps you have open, by name: pick one and the widget follows that app, at its top right corner, and hides when you minimize it. While you arrange them, an attached widget shows Back on the desktop. You can also ask Bit "keep the timer on Zoom" or "put my notes on Excel". While you arrange them, those windows take every click; press Done, or leave it for ten minutes, and the screen behaves as before. Your widgets can also live on pages, for example Work and Games: while you arrange them, press New page in the bar, then tap a page to show its widgets. Tap the page already shown to rename it, delete it, or mark it When I play: while a game runs, Xenon shows that page, and goes back to the page you had when the game ends. A page can also follow a virtual desktop: tap it, choose Show on a desktop and pick a desktop, and switching to that desktop shows its widgets, while switching away brings back the page you had. Every desktop undoes it, and Bit understands "show Work on desktop 2". This works on Windows, on a Mac (Beta) and on Linux in an X11 session (Beta). You can also ask Bit "show my work widgets" or "make a Games page", or switch page with the new Deck key Widgets on screen: change page, which goes to the next page when no page is chosen. On a Mac and on Linux, see Widgets on your screen on macOS (Beta) and on Linux (Beta) below.

  • Your Ambient scene as the desktop wallpaper, or as the PC screensaver

    In the Xenon app on Windows, Settings → Ambient has a new block, On the PC. Animated desktop wallpaper puts the scene you picked behind your desktop icons; it stops while you play, while a window fills the screen, on battery and in Remote Desktop. PC screensaver shows the scene full screen after 5 to 60 minutes without using the PC, and any key, click or mouse move closes it; it never starts during a game, a video that keeps the screen on, or a full screen window. It goes on the screens without the dashboard, or on your only screen. Both start off. You can also ask Bit "turn on the animated wallpaper" or "start the screensaver after 10 minutes", and the wallpaper has a Deck key. Widgets made for Ambient scenes learn where they are (placement.where is wallpaper or screensaver), so they can skip asking for a tap. On a Mac and on Linux both work too (Beta). On Linux they need an X11 session with a compositor running, or KDE Plasma, Sway or Hyprland on Wayland with the gtk-layer-shell library installed; there the wallpaper sits under your windows instead of behind the icons, so on desktops that draw their own icons (KDE Plasma, Xfce) it can cover them, and Settings says so; it stops on battery and while a window fills the screen. Not on GNOME with Wayland, where the block does not appear.

  • Use Xenon without the dashboard

    Settings, General, How you use Xenon has three choices: Dashboard (as before), Widgets only, and Both. A new install asks once and marks a recommended choice: Both with a second screen, Dashboard on a lone Xeneon Edge, Widgets only otherwise. If you update, nothing is asked and nothing moves: you are on Both, and the widgets are there when you want them. With Widgets only the app keeps no dashboard window at all, not even a hidden one: your widgets stay on the screen, the search shortcut still opens the search, and the app uses less memory. The switch happens at once. The tray's Show Xenon, or opening Xenon by hand, still shows the dashboard, in a normal window on the screen you are on, with the Store, Sparks and every setting; closing it goes back to widgets only. You can also ask Bit "I only want the widgets" or use the new Deck key How you use Xenon. Bit still answers "Hey Xenon" in Widgets only, while the on-screen alerts are on: it talks in a card at the bottom of your main screen, the same one the dashboard shows in its see-through voice mode, and the screen edges light up as set in Settings, Xenon AI. A Deck key set to talk to Bit by voice does the same. Bit loads only when you call it and gives the memory back a minute after you finish. What only the dashboard can do, such as changing its theme or opening a page of it, Bit says needs the dashboard instead of saying it is done, and a card on the screen opens it; Voce Live needs the dashboard too. With the on-screen alerts off, the wake word is off. The pop-ups the dashboard shows still reach you: a saved screenshot, recording or replay, a timer that ends, a Guardian warning, a benchmark result, a stock or football alert, a UniFi event, a calendar reminder, a Deck shortcut that failed, the minute before an automatic update and a new version of Xenon appear at the top right of your main screen, an incoming call shows the same call card as on the dashboard, with its ring, with their sounds, and clicks next to them reach whatever is underneath. Tapping the new version card opens the dashboard and installs it; asking Bit or a Deck key for the gallery opens the dashboard with the gallery. The app itself keeps updating with the dashboard, as it does with Dashboard chosen. They follow your Notifications settings, and Settings, Notifications, On-screen alerts in widgets only turns them off (or ask Bit "stop the pop-ups on my screen"). In the Windows app, and in the Mac and Linux apps as a Beta (see Widgets on your screen on macOS and on Linux).

  • The Xenon menu, over any app

    In the Xenon app, press Alt+Shift+X in any app, games in a borderless window included, and one menu opens in a window of its own that you move, resize and minimize like any other: the app under it stays visible and keeps working, and the window comes back where you left it. It stays on top only while a game is on; anywhere else it goes behind the app you click, and Alt+Shift+X brings it back. A link in the menu opens in your browser with the menu left open under it, and the menu comes back on top when you return to it. A search field at the top finds any function or setting by name. It has everything Xenon does on your screen: Now (every function in groups: capture, performance, tools, Bit, the Store and Sparks, with their key combination when they have one, and whether Instant Replay is on), Widgets (add any tile or Store widget from a list that shows a picture or an icon of each one and says in a line what it does; for each one choose where it sits, on the desktop under your windows, above everything, or on an app it follows, on which screen, and when it shows; switch, rename and delete pages; edit; small moving pictures show what each place and a page mean), Capture (what a recording takes and Instant Replay, with a moving picture of where the webcam goes; the rest is in Settings), Shortcuts and macros (every key combination in one place, the ones that clash with another app named, and a new shortcut or macro for any function, made in the same window), Look (theme, animated wallpaper and the scene it shows, screensaver) and How you use Xenon. Settings, the Store, Sparks, the gallery, the mixer and the chat with Bit, by writing or by voice, open inside the same window, and Settings shows only what applies to how you use Xenon. With Widgets only nothing in the menu opens the dashboard. Above everything the performance readings are words only, with no box behind them, one reading per line, and you choose the readings. Every function says in one short line what it is for, in every language, and the search finds those words too. Press the same keys or Esc, or its X, to close it. Widgets and cards on the screen no longer stop Chrome, Edge and apps built on them from drawing what sits under them: a page opened there used to stay blank. A function that works on the screen, such as Screenshot, the colour picker or the ruler, moves the menu out of the picture and brings it back when it ends, with a line at the top saying what happened: for a screenshot its picture, its size, and the buttons to open or pin it, so with several monitors you see which one it took. Mark the moment says what it does right now: with Instant Replay on it saves a clip of what just happened, during a recording it leaves a mark you can find later, and with neither on it takes you to the Instant Replay switch. The Store and Sparks, with how many Sparks you have, stay in the sidebar whatever section is open. The keys can be changed in the menu itself, and Settings, General and the menu on the dashboard show them, so whoever found the menu by a button learns the shortcut too. It also opens from the tray (Open Xenon menu), from Settings, General, from the new Deck key Xenon menu, or by asking Bit "open the Xenon menu". The dashboard has the same menu, with the same sections, so whoever uses Xenon on a second screen or a phone controls the main screen from there: the new Main screen tile shows the capture buttons, the widgets on the screen and their status, and opens the whole menu. The first time the app starts on a PC where it can draw on the screen, after the question about which screen to use, it asks once how you want to use Xenon, in words about your screens (I have a second screen, I have one screen, dashboard on one and widgets on the other), with the second screen already chosen, and it shows the keys of the menu. This also reaches anyone who already has Xenon installed. If you pick widgets, the menu opens once by itself; the guided tour follows only if you keep a dashboard. Store widgets with the permission to show or hide your widgets can open it too (they see nothing in it). In the Windows app, and in the Mac and Linux apps as a Beta.

  • A key combination for each widget on your screen

    In the Xenon menu, open Adjust on a widget and set a key combination under Keys. Choose how it works: press it to show or hide the widget, or hold it to see the widget only while you hold the keys, for example a clock or your FPS over a game. On Linux, where the system does not say when the keys are let go, holding shows the widget for four seconds. Store widgets can also put their own functions on key combinations, such as Next lap on a stopwatch: they are listed in the same card, and only functions that need no settings and that you have allowed can go on a key. A widget can suggest a combination; Xenon shows it as a suggestion and nothing is set until you accept it. Every widget key appears in Shortcuts and macros with the others, and a combination already in use is refused with the name of what holds it. Creators set the suggestion with key in the manifest and key on each Deck function (see the SDK guide); the Maker has both. In the Windows app, and in the Mac and Linux apps as a Beta.

  • Ctrl+Alt with a letter works when your keyboard allows it

    On many keyboards Ctrl+Alt is AltGr and types characters such as €, so Xenon refused every Ctrl+Alt letter as a shortcut. On Windows it now checks the keyboards installed on your PC and takes Ctrl+Alt+R and the others that none of them uses to type something; Ctrl+Alt+E stays refused on an Italian keyboard, where it types €. When a combination is held by another app on the PC, recording a shortcut now says so instead of staying silent. On macOS and Linux every Ctrl+Alt letter is still refused.

  • Claude Code's questions take the screen, like its permission requests

    A question from Claude waited on the Claude Code tile for four minutes and never opened full screen, so it was easy to miss; the terminal shows nothing while it waits there. Now, if it is not answered within 25 seconds, it opens full screen with its options, and it waits nine minutes as a permission request does. If it goes to the terminal (you tap In the terminal, press Esc, or time runs out), the tile says it is waiting for your answer in the terminal and shows the question, instead of "Waiting for your approval".

  • The "widget using a lot of resources" warning blames the right widget

    Xenon measures how long each Store widget keeps the screen busy. On some setups it also counted the time the dashboard itself was busy, for example while it reloaded after a restart, so a quiet widget such as a Discord one could get the warning. Only the widget's own work counts now.

  • Put a widget on your screen right after installing it

    When a widget from the Store or from a share link is installed, the same notice now has a Put on screen button: it lands at the top right, and Move lets you drag it where you want. With Widgets only it is the one choice offered, and a pack with several widgets opens the list so you choose. In Xenon Maker the install window has a Put on screen link that installs your widget and places it in one go. In the Windows app, and in the Mac and Linux apps as a Beta.

  • The minute before an automatic update shows again

    With automatic updates on, Xenon is meant to warn you a minute before it restarts to update, with a button to wait an hour. That warning never appeared, so the app updated without notice. It now shows on the dashboard, and in widgets only at the top right of your screen, and In an hour moves the update by an hour.

  • Calendar reminders ring once

    With the dashboard open on two screens (the Edge and a phone, say), each one used to ring the same reminder, and a reminder for a subscribed calendar could ring again on every device. Xenon now decides when a reminder is due in one place and every open screen shows the same one, once. The lights flash once too.

  • The edges of your screens light up while you talk to Bit

    In the Xenon app on Windows, a voice chat now makes the border of the screen you called Bit from glow, in the same colours as the dashboard's own glow: the accent colour while Bit listens and speaks, lavender while it thinks. That is the dashboard's screen, or the main screen when you use widgets only. Choose where in Settings → Bit → Glowing edge: the screen you call Bit from (the default), the main screen, the second screen, every screen, or off.
