You can also ask Bit "light up every screen when we talk". The glow never takes a click, does not show in screenshots or recordings, and goes away the moment the chat ends. On a Mac and on Linux it works too, as a Beta that has not been tried on real hardware yet: on Linux it works where widgets on your screen work, so not on GNOME with Wayland or without a compositor (Settings says why), and there it can show in screenshots and recordings, because Linux has no way to keep a window out of them.

  • Ask Bit how your game is running

    Ask "how is my game running?" and Bit answers with the game's average FPS, its 1% and 0.1% lows (how low the frame rate drops at its worst moments) and its slowest frame time, measured on the frames of the last few seconds. The lows only appear once enough frames have been seen, so a number is never a guess. Windows only for now, where Xenon measures every frame; on macOS and Linux the AI is not offered it.

  • Game performance tile

    A new tile shows the frame rate of the game you are playing, its 1% and 0.1% lows, the frame time, and a line of the latest frames where a stutter shows up as a spike, with CPU and GPU load and the GPU temperature underneath. Add it from the dashboard's tile list, or, in the Xenon app on Windows, put it over your game: ask Bit "show my FPS over the game". It updates four times a second, and only while a game runs and the tile is on a screen; the rest of the time it sends nothing. Without a game it says so in one line. When a game runs but its frames cannot be read, the tile names the game and says why instead of asking you to start one, and on Windows it tells you when PresentMon still needs installing from Settings. When a game runs in exclusive full screen, where no window can show over it, the tile says so, and if you have widgets over the game a message tells you once per game to switch it to borderless or windowed full screen in its display settings. Bit knows it too. On Windows Xenon measures every frame. On Linux the frame rate needs the game started with MangoHud, and the tile says so. On macOS the tile explains that one app cannot measure the frame rate of another there. Over a game it shows numbers only: warnings and hints stay on the dashboard tile and with Bit, never on top of what you are playing.

  • Choose what the Game performance tile shows

    The row of this widget in the Widgets section of the Xenon menu and Settings, Performance, Game performance list every reading in four groups, with a switch each: while you play (FPS, 1% low, 0.1% low, frame time, frame graph), CPU (use, temperature, clock, power), GPU (use, temperature, clock, power, video memory), memory and network (RAM, ping, packet loss). What you turn off is gone from the tile, on the dashboard and over the game alike. Ping and packet loss are measured to the internet (1.1.1.1), not to the game's server. Over a game the tile is words only, with a thin dark edge so they stay readable on any picture, and Small, Medium and Large change the size of the text, not of a box. The words sit flush with the edge of the screen you picked, and clicks go through them to whatever is underneath. You can also ask Bit, for example "add the CPU temperature to the FPS tile". Until you change it the tile shows what it showed before.

  • Remove the background of a widget on your screen

    In the Xenon menu, Widgets, every tile or widget with a panel has Remove background, so only its content stays on the desktop or over the game. Put it back from the same row, or ask Bit ("take the background off the music widget"). With a Store widget or one you made, that shows words alone if the widget itself has a transparent background. It works on the widget you placed, so the same widget keeps its panel on the dashboard.

  • Games played, compared

    Xenon now remembers each game you play for more than two minutes: average FPS, 1% and 0.1% lows, how long you played, average CPU and GPU load and the peak temperatures. Between games the Game performance tile shows the last one and says how it went against the time before, for example "12 FPS more than the one before". Ask Bit "how did my last game go?" or "did the driver update help?". The newest 100 games are kept on this PC and go into the backup. Settings, Performance, Games played lists the last ten, each with how it went against the time before in the same game, so a driver update or a patch shows up without picking anything; turn it off or delete them there too. On Linux it records the average only; on macOS there is no frame rate to record, so the option is not shown.

  • Benchmark

    A new Deck key, in the Performance group, records the time of every frame of the game you are playing and saves it as a CSV file in Documents, Xenon, Benchmark. The key stays lit while it records, whoever started it. Press it again to stop, or say "start a benchmark" and "stop the benchmark" to Bit. While it records, the Game performance tile shows "Benchmark" with the time; when it stops, a message gives the average FPS and the 1% low with a button to show the file. A run also stops by itself when the game closes or after 30 minutes. Windows only, because it needs the frame times PresentMon measures.

  • Screenshot

    A new Deck key, in the new Capture group, saves what is on your screen as a PNG in Pictures, Xenon, in a folder named after the game you are playing (or Desktop), and copies it, ready to paste, as Win+Shift+S does. It takes the whole monitor you are working on, only the window in front, or an area you pick: the screen freezes and you drag a rectangle or click a window. Esc or the right mouse button cancels. On an HDR screen the picture comes out with the same colors you see, instead of washed out or too dark. A message confirms it with a button to show the file. You can also ask Bit to "take a screenshot". Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Copy text from the screen

    A new Deck key, in the Capture group, reads the words on your screen and puts them on the clipboard, ready to paste: from a scanned PDF, a picture, a video or an app that does not let you select. The screen freezes, you drag over the text (or click a window), and a message says how many lines were copied. The key can also read the window in front or the whole screen without asking for an area. You can ask Bit "copy the text of this window" or "what does this error say?": Bit reads it and can answer about it. The text goes only to the clipboard of this PC, and to the AI you use for Bit when you ask Bit: a paired phone or a widget that presses the key gets only the number of lines, and a widget can only start a read of an area you drag. It uses the text recognition built into Windows, in the languages installed in Settings, Time and language, Language; if none of them has it, the key says so. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Pin a screenshot on the screen

    A new Deck key, in the Capture group, keeps a picture on top of your windows, like a sticky note: drag over an area and it stays there, to copy numbers from it into a form or to keep a reference image over a drawing app. Drag it to move it, use the mouse wheel to make it bigger or smaller, Ctrl and the wheel to make it see-through, and the x on it to take it away. The key can also pin your last screenshot, a "Pin" button sits on the "Screenshot saved" message and in the gallery, and you can ask Bit to "pin this on the screen". It can go on the desktop under your windows instead. Deleting the screenshot in the gallery takes its pin away too. A widget can start one only from an area you drag. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Edit a screenshot before you share it

    In the gallery, an "Edit" button on every screenshot opens a simple editor: arrows, boxes, text, a highlighter and black covers. "Find private data" looks for e-mail addresses, IBANs and long numbers (phone, card or account numbers) with your PC's own text recognition, nothing leaves the PC, and covers them; tap a cover to take it away, Undo takes back the last step. "Save copy" saves a new screenshot next to the original, which stays as it was. It does not find names, addresses or faces, so check the copy and cover those by hand. A new Deck key, "Cover private data", and Bit ("cover the private data in my last screenshot") make a covered copy in one step. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Bug report in one press

    A new Deck key in the Capture group, "Bug report", and Bit ("make a bug report") put what a developer needs into one .zip: a picture of the window in front, the last 10, 30 or 60 seconds of the screen when Instant Replay is on, a short system.txt (Xenon version, system, CPU, RAM, GPU, the app in front) and a README that says what is inside and what is missing. In Settings → Capture → Bug report you choose where the packages go (Documents\Xenon\Bug reports until you change it) and, if you want, a folder of logs: its newest files go in too, up to 20 files and 50 MB. The package never holds your PC's name, a window title or a file path. Two presses in the same second make two packages, the second named "(2)". The notice says what went in, and Show opens the folder. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Why does it stutter?

    A new Deck key in the Performance group, "Why does it stutter?", and Bit ("why does my game stutter?") answer from what Xenon already measures while a game runs: the frame times of the last seconds, the graphics card and processor load, the busiest core, video and system memory and the temperatures. The answer is one cause and one next step, for example "Video memory full: lower texture quality or resolution", "Graphics card at full load", "Capped at 60 FPS" (V-Sync or a frame limit, which is normal) or "Loading stutter" when nothing is at its limit. It runs on your PC with fixed rules, no AI model and nothing sent anywhere; Bit only puts it in words. While the game stutters, the Game performance tile shows the cause in one line under the graph, and widgets with the perf permission get it too. Windows only, because it needs single frame times.

  • Timelapse

    A new Deck key in the Capture group, "Timelapse", records the screen or the window in front as a sped-up video: one picture every 1, 2, 5, 10, 30 or 60 seconds, played at 30 pictures a second, so an hour at one picture every 2 seconds becomes a one-minute video. Made for drawing, building or a long session you want to show. It has no sound and lands next to your recordings with "Timelapse" in its name; when it ends, Xenon says how long it watched and how long the video is. Bit starts it too ("make a timelapse of my drawing, one picture every 10 seconds"). Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Webcam in your recordings

    The "Record video" key has a new "Webcam" choice: pick a corner and your camera appears in a round bubble in that corner of the video, for tutorials and commentary. It is off unless you choose it, the camera turns on only while that recording runs, and if no camera can be opened the video goes on without it and Xenon says so. Bit does it too ("record the screen with my webcam in the bottom right"). Not in a timelapse. Also on macOS (Beta), see below.

  • Send a capture to your phone

    In the gallery, a screenshot or a video now has a "To phone" button: it appears on your paired phone in the File transfer tile, ready to download, over your home network with no account and nothing uploaded. Your phone gets the same notification as any file sent from the PC, if you turned it on in Settings, Phone. The file stays where it is on the PC. A new Deck key, "Send to phone", sends your newest screenshot or video, and Bit does it too ("send the last clip to my phone"). The button shows only while a phone is paired and file transfer is on; a file over the transfer limit asks you to trim it or make a lighter copy first. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta).

  • Copies of a video for phones and chats

    In the gallery, a video now has an "Export" button with three choices. Vertical 9:16 makes a tall copy for TikTok, Shorts and Reels: you pick which part of the picture to keep (left, centre or right), and a recording with your webcam can put the camera on top and the game below. Lighter makes a copy that fits a size, 10, 25, 50 or 100 MB, so it can go into a chat that limits uploads. GIF makes a GIF without sound, 480 px on its long side; a long clip gets a warning that the GIF may come out heavy, instead of a fixed limit. The copy lands beside the original, which stays as it is, and you can stop it while it is being made. A video that is already smaller than the size you pick is left alone, and Xenon tells you to send it as it is. A new Deck key, "Export the last video", does the same for your latest recording or replay clip, and Bit does it too ("make a vertical copy of my last clip", "make it small enough for a chat"). Everything happens on this PC. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Videos with a transcript and chapters

    In the gallery, a recording or Instant Replay clip now has a "Transcript" button: Xenon writes down what is said, on this PC with the same local speech recognition as the voice (Settings, Bit, Whisper), so nothing is uploaded. Tap a line to jump the video there; the line being said is marked while it plays. "Chapters with Bit" asks Bit to write a short summary and chapters, which then show above the text. "Subtitles (.srt)" saves a subtitle file for any video player or editor. You can also just ask Bit: "what did I say in the last video?" or "split my recording into chapters". A paired phone can read a transcript that already exists. Videos up to 2 hours; Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Record the steps of a procedure

    A new Deck key, "Record steps", and Bit ("record the steps") start it: every click takes a picture of that screen with a red ring where you clicked, and notes what you clicked and in which app. A small pill at the top of the screen counts the steps; click it to finish. Where there is no pill, a card with Stop does the same. What you type is never recorded, only that you typed something, so the document says "then type the text". At the end Xenon writes the steps in Documents\Xenon\Steps: a page with the pictures inside that opens in any browser, prints and can be sent as one file, plus a Markdown copy for a wiki. It stops by itself at 100 steps or after 20 minutes without a click. Ask Bit to write the procedure up in your own words after you stop. Nothing leaves the PC. On Windows, and on Linux with X11 (Beta, see Screenshots and recordings on Linux).

  • Draw on the screen

    A new Deck key in the Capture group lays a see-through sheet over the monitor you are working on, so you can point at things while you present, teach or record a video. A small bar at the top picks the color (red, yellow, green, blue, white, black) and the tool: pen, highlighter, arrow or box. Shift draws a straight line, Ctrl a box, Ctrl+Shift an arrow; Ctrl+Z undoes, E clears, Esc or the x on the bar closes it. Your drawing shows in screenshots and recordings, the bar does not. Nothing is saved. You can also ask Bit to "let me draw on the screen", and a widget can open it. On a Mac and on Linux (Beta) the sheet opens on your main screen with the same bar, colours, tools and keys; there the bar shows in screenshots and recordings too. On Linux it works where widgets on your screen work (see Widgets on your screen on Linux).

  • Color picker and ruler

    Two new Deck keys in the Capture group. The color picker freezes your screens and shows a magnifier under the mouse: click a pixel and its color goes on the clipboard as HEX (#1E90FF), RGB or HSL, whichever you choose on the key. The ruler lets you drag over anything on the screen and copies its size in pixels (333 × 177). A message shows what was copied; Esc or a right click cancels. You can also ask Bit "what color is this?" or "how big is this window?". A widget can start them, but never learns the color or the size. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Record video

    A new Deck key, in the Capture group, records the whole monitor you are working on or only the window in front, as an MP4 in Videos, Xenon, in a folder named after the game (or Desktop). Press it to start and again to stop; the key stays lit while it records, whoever started it. A small pill with a red dot and the time sits at the top of the screen being recorded, even with no dashboard open: click its square to stop. With the pill there is no card as well; if you hid the pill, the dashboard shows a Recording message with a Stop button. It never takes the focus and never appears in your videos or screenshots. Recording a window stops by itself when the window closes. When it ends, a message gives the length with a button to show the file. You can also say "record the window in front" and "stop recording" to Bit. If Xenon closes or crashes during a recording, the part already recorded is kept and plays. On an HDR screen the colors come out as you see them. The video has sound: recording a window keeps only the sound of that app (no notifications or music from other apps), recording the screen keeps everything the PC plays. The key's Audio choice can add your microphone, for a commentary or a tutorial, or record no sound at all; the microphone is never on unless you choose it. With the microphone, the file has one track with everything mixed, which every player plays, plus the PC sound and the microphone on their own tracks for editing. If Windows does not allow the microphone, the Recording message says so and the video goes on without it. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Recording options

    Settings now has a Capture page, with the recording options: 60 or 30 frames per second, the size (as the screen, 1440p, 1080p or 720p), the quality (normal, high for bigger files, small for sharing), whether the time pill shows on the screen, the folder and a space limit. The folder is chosen with the system's folder window, and Back to Videos undoes it; if the folder is gone (an unplugged drive), the recording goes to Videos and the message says so. With a limit (10 to 100 GB), after each recording Xenon deletes its oldest recordings until the rest fit, never the one just made and never files it did not record; the page shows how much they take now. You can also ask Bit "record at 30 fps", "hide the recording pill" or "keep my recordings under 50 GB". On a paired phone the page only says these are changed on the PC. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Instant Replay

    Turn it on in Settings, Capture, and Xenon keeps the last minutes of your screen, so a moment you did not plan to record is not lost. To save them, press Ctrl+Shift+F10 in any app, tap the new Instant Replay key in the Deck's Capture group, or say "save the last 30 seconds" to Bit. The clip is saved as an MP4 in Videos, Xenon, in a folder named after the game, in about a second, and a message confirms it with a button to show the file. Choose how much it keeps, from 15 seconds to 60 minutes (Other takes any length in minutes); the page shows how much disk space that takes, and warns when the disk does not have it. A Deck key can also save only the last part, for example the last 30 seconds out of 5 minutes kept. By default it runs only while a game is open, starting and stopping by itself; choose Always to keep the desktop too. Sound can be the PC sound, the PC sound and your microphone, or none; the microphone is never on unless you choose it. The Deck key stays lit while the replay is running, and if it cannot start the page says why. The shortcut can be changed or turned off on the same page, with the same rules as Deck key shortcuts; it is held only while Instant Replay is on, so otherwise the combination stays free for other apps. You can also ask Bit "turn on instant replay", "keep the last 5 minutes" or "save the replay with Alt+Shift+R". It is off by default, because while it is on it records all the time. The kept minutes wait on the disk, not in memory, and are deleted as new ones arrive. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Choose where things are saved

    Each folder sits with what it saves: screenshots and videos in Settings, Capture, benchmark files in Settings, Performance, Benchmark. Each is picked with the Windows folder window and has its own Back to button. If a chosen folder is gone, the file goes to the usual place (Videos, Pictures or Documents) and the message says so. Exporting a backup, a shared preset or a share card now opens a Save as window in the browser, so you choose the folder and the name; where the browser has no such window, it downloads as before. In the iCUE view the backup asks for the folder with the Windows folder window. The folder where files from your phone arrive is also picked with the Windows folder window instead of typing the path. You can ask Bit "save my screenshots in another folder" too. Folders on this PC are never chosen from a paired phone.

  • Gallery

    Your screenshots, recordings and saved replays now have their own gallery: open it from Settings, Capture, from the Open button on the message that confirms a capture, from the new Gallery key in the Deck's Capture group (it can open on videos or screenshots only), or ask Bit "show me my clips". Captures are grouped by day, newest first, with the game's name, the time and the length on every clip; filters show only videos or only screenshots, or only one game. Tap a capture to see it large, and move to the next one with the arrows on screen or on the keyboard. Trim a video by dragging its two handles (or with the arrow keys): the trimmed copy is saved next to the original in about a second, because nothing is encoded again, so nothing is lost in quality; the original stays. The copy starts at the nearest keyframe, at most one second before the point you chose, and the page says so. Copy puts the file itself on the clipboard, ready to paste into a chat, a mail or a folder, videos included. Show in folder opens it in Explorer, and Delete asks for a second tap. The header shows how much space your captures take. On a paired phone the gallery opens too: look at your captures, download them, and make a trimmed copy, a copy for sharing or a transcript, which the PC makes and keeps beside the original; copying to the PC's clipboard, Show in folder and deleting stay on the PC. Bit can also list your latest captures and tell you, for example, which game the last clip is from. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta), see below.

  • Mark a moment while you record

    While a recording or Instant Replay runs, the new Deck key "Mark this moment" (Capture group), Bit ("mark this moment") or a Store widget with the capture permission drops a bookmark on it; a short notice confirms it, with the time when a recording runs. When nothing is recording, the key says so instead. On Windows, Xenon also marks by itself the spots where a game's FPS suddenly drop, at most one every 20 seconds and never in the first 10 seconds of a game, so the stutter you want to look at is easy to find; turn it off in Settings, Capture, "Mark where the game stutters". In the gallery, the marks of a video show as buttons under it: a tap jumps to two seconds before the spot and plays. A trimmed copy keeps the marks inside it. Also on macOS and Linux (Beta) for your own bookmarks; the automatic stutter marks need the frame times Xenon reads on Windows.

  • Clips from your marks

    With Instant Replay on, every moment you mark becomes a clip by itself: 15 seconds before the mark to 5 after, saved in the gallery a few seconds later, with a short notice. Marks close together share one clip, up to a minute. In Settings, Capture, "Automatic clips" also offers "Also where the game stutters" (silent, at most one clip every 2 minutes) and "Never"; nothing is cut while a recording runs, because the recording already holds the moment. For a video you already saved, "Clips from marks" in the gallery (also on the phone), the Deck key of the same name or Bit ("make clips from my marks") cuts a clip around each mark next to the original, which stays as it is, at most 20 at a time, without re-encoding. Where the gallery can trim: Windows, and macOS and Linux (Beta).

  • Widgets can take screenshots and start recordings (for widget makers)

    A new SDK permission, Screenshots, recordings and the replay (capture), lets a widget take a screenshot, start or stop a recording and save the Instant Replay, the same as a Deck key. The widget never sees the picture, the video or where they are saved; it only learns whether it worked. It can only start these: showing the file, turning Instant Replay on or off and recording the microphone are refused. The person installing the widget sees the permission in the install dialog. The SDK guide has the details.

  • Screenshots and recordings on macOS (Beta)

    On a Mac, Xenon now fetches its capture engine by itself the first time it starts, checked against the same signed list as on Windows, and the Capture keys work there too: a screenshot of the screen, of the window in front or of an area you drag, a recording of the screen or of a window with the microphone if you want it, Copy text from the screen, and the gallery with trim, copy, Show in folder and Transcript. The first time, macOS asks you to allow Screen Recording for Xenon (and the Microphone, if you record it). The computer's own sound in recordings (macOS 13 or later), the recording's frame rate, size and quality, timelapse, the colour picker, the ruler (drag over what you want to measure with the Mac's own area picker), covering private data and the copies for phones and chats work there too. Instant Replay works on a Mac too (macOS 12.3 or later): the last minutes wait on disk in your Library's Caches folder, saving a clip does not stop it, and it uses the same Screen Recording permission (and the Microphone, if you add it). The webcam bubble works on a Mac too (macOS 12.3 or later): the first time, macOS asks you to allow the Camera, and if no camera answers the recording goes on without it and the card says so. The step recorder works on a Mac too: the first time, macOS asks you to allow Input Monitoring for Xenon so it can see your clicks; after you allow it, start the recorder again. What you type is never recorded, only that you typed. To name the buttons you click, also allow Accessibility for Xenon in System Settings, Privacy & Security; without it each step points to the circled spot. There is no counter on the screen: the capture card shows that it runs. Drawing on the screen works on a Mac too (see Draw on the screen). It has not been tried on a real Mac yet, so tell us what does not work. On Linux, see Screenshots and recordings on Linux (Beta).

  • Widgets on your screen on macOS (Beta)

    In the Xenon app on a Mac, widgets can now go on the desktop and over everything, as on Windows: ask Bit "put the weather on the desktop, top right", arrange them with Edit the widgets on screen, group them as tabs and use pages. Widgets only in Settings, General works there too, with the on-screen alerts and Bit's voice card. On the desktop the widgets sit under your windows and stay on every Space; clicks next to a widget reach whatever is underneath. The animated wallpaper and the screensaver from Settings, Ambient work there too, and so do the glowing screen edges while you talk to Bit. A widget can also go next to an app, as on Windows: it follows the front window of that app and hides when the app is closed, minimized, hidden or on another Space. Clicking a widget makes Xenon the active app, so click your game or app again before you type in it. It has not been tried on a real Mac yet, so tell us what does not work.

  • Widgets on your screen on Linux (Beta)

    In the Xenon app on Linux, widgets can go on the desktop and over everything in an X11 session with a compositor running: ask Bit "put the weather on the desktop, top right", arrange them with Edit the widgets on screen, group them as tabs and use pages. Widgets only in Settings, General works there too, with the on-screen alerts and Bit's voice card. Desktop widgets sit under your windows and stay on every workspace; clicks next to a widget reach whatever is underneath, and a widget never takes the keyboard. A game in full screen can still cover the widgets over everything, because the window manager decides that. On KDE Plasma, Sway and Hyprland with Wayland they work too, when the gtk-layer-shell library is installed. On GNOME with Wayland an app cannot put its own windows under or over the others, so the option is not offered and Settings says why; the same on X11 without a compositor, where the widgets would sit on a black box. The animated wallpaper and the PC screensaver work there too (see the Ambient entry), and so do the glowing screen edges while you talk to Bit, which can show in screenshots and recordings there. A widget can also go next to an app in an X11 session: it follows the front window of that app and hides when the app is closed, minimized or on another workspace. On Wayland the system does not tell an app where the other windows are, so the option is not offered there and Bit says why. It has not been tried on a real Linux PC yet, so tell us what does not work.

  • Screenshots and recordings on Linux (Beta)

    On Linux, Xenon now fetches its capture engine by itself, checked against the same signed list as on Windows and macOS, and the engine uses the tools of your desktop, so what you get depends on what is installed. On an X11 session, with maim (or ImageMagick's import), xdotool and ffmpeg: screenshots of the screen, of the window in front or of an area you drag, recordings of the screen or of a window with the computer's sound and the microphone. On Sway, Hyprland and the other wlroots desktops, with grim, slurp and wf-recorder: screenshots of the screen or of an area, and recordings of the screen or of an area with the microphone. On KDE and GNOME with Wayland, with Spectacle or GNOME Screenshot: screenshots; recordings of the screen, with the computer's sound and the microphone, work too when ffmpeg and the GStreamer PipeWire plugin are installed. There the desktop asks which screen to share the first time, and remembers the answer; stopping the share from the desktop ends the recording and keeps the file. Instant Replay, timelapse and recording a single window are not available there. Everywhere, Copy text from the screen works when tesseract is installed, the gallery's previews, trim and Transcript need ffmpeg, and Copy needs wl-clipboard or xclip, and choosing a folder in Settings needs zenity or kdialog. Screenshots and videos go to the Pictures and Videos folders your desktop names in its own language (for example ~/Immagini). With ffmpeg, on X11 and on the wlroots desktops, Instant Replay, timelapse, the recording's frame rate, size and quality, covering private data and the copies for phones and chats work too; the kept minutes of Instant Replay wait in your cache folder (~/.cache/xenon/Replay), not in memory. The colour picker and the ruler work on X11 (with xdotool and ImageMagick or ffmpeg) and on the wlroots desktops (with slurp and grim). The step recorder works on X11 (with xinput, xdotool, ffmpeg and maim or ImageMagick): there each step names the app you clicked but not the button, and the card on the dashboard shows that it runs instead of a pill on the screen. Not on Wayland, where apps cannot see clicks made in other apps. Drawing on the screen works where widgets on your screen work (see Draw on the screen). What your PC cannot do does not appear. On SteamOS in Game Mode nothing can be drawn or captured over the game, so use the Desktop Mode. Tried on X11, Sway and GNOME sessions in a test machine, not yet on a real Linux PC, so tell us what does not work.

  • Hide only the widgets over the game

    Press Ctrl+Shift+F9 to hide the widgets you put over everything, and press it again to bring them back. The widgets on your desktop stay where they are. The shortcut works only while at least one widget is over everything, so it takes nothing from other apps the rest of the time. You can change it or turn it off by asking Bit ("change the overlay shortcut to Alt+Shift+O"). The Deck key Widgets on screen: show or hide now has a Which widgets option: All, Over the game or On the desktop. On a Mac and on Linux (Beta) it works like the other Xenon shortcuts: on a Mac with the Xenon Helper, on Linux added by itself on GNOME, and on other desktops you add it in your keyboard settings as Xenon explains.

  • More of the Deck for widgets

    With your permission, a widget can now start its own timers and stopwatches, change Wave Link mixes and effects, move Wave Link to another output device, and pick a SignalRGB effect. A widget's timers show on the Timers tile with the widget's name in front, up to 5 each, and it cannot see, restart or stop yours.

  • Deck keys on your screen

    Any Deck key can now sit on your screen as a small button, over your windows or on the desktop, so you can turn the lights on or start a Streamer.bot action with one click even with a single monitor. In the key editor, under What it does, press Put on the screen; in edit mode it is under Add; or ask Bit. A key Bit placed shows you every step first and runs only after you allow it, and a key you edit later asks again. Widgets cannot place or press these keys, and phones cannot either.

  • Keyboard shortcuts for Deck keys

    Any Deck key can now run from a keyboard shortcut, from whatever app you are in. In the key editor, under What it does, press Record and then the combination you want, for example Ctrl+Shift+F9. The key runs all its actions in order, with their delays, exactly as if you had tapped it. Combinations that Windows, NVIDIA, Xbox Game Bar or other common apps already use are refused with the reason, and so is one that another key or a page shortcut already has. Under the button you see whether the shortcut works right now, or why not (for example, another app took it first). You can also ask Bit "put Ctrl+Shift+F9 on my Music key" or "which shortcuts do I have?". Sound steps play on the dashboard open on this PC; with none open, the PC plays them itself (mp3, wav, m4a and flac on Windows and macOS, the system's PipeWire or PulseAudio player on Linux, any other format with ffplay, which comes with ffmpeg). With Widgets only, an app volume step opens the dashboard on the mixer, a Bit chat or question step opens it on the chat with the question asked, and a Bit voice step opens Bit on the screen. Xenon can hold 16 shortcuts in all, counting the search and page shortcuts. It needs Xenon Helper on Windows and macOS, and GNOME on Linux. Deck codes you share do not carry shortcuts.

  • Game Companion on your main screen

    With Widgets only there is no dashboard and no button over the game, so Game Companion now opens from a Deck key (Bit group), from that key's keyboard shortcut, or by asking Bit "open the game companion". The card appears in the middle of the main screen with the game, how long you have been playing and the FPS; clicking it never takes the focus from the game, and every click outside the card goes to the game. Since that window cannot type, "Ask out loud" takes the place of the question box and hands over to Bit's voice. With Widgets only, Xenon's cards on the main screen (alerts, Bit, Game Companion) stay out of screenshots and recordings, and Bit does not see them when it looks at your screen. Game Companion stays off until you turn it on in Settings, Bit, Advanced AI features; the key says so if it is off, or if on-screen alerts are turned off. A Store widget allowed to show or hide your widgets on the screen can open it too, for a "Companion" button; it learns nothing about the game.

  • Lights follow the album cover with Widgets only too

    The Lighting effect that takes its colours from the album cover only worked while the dashboard was open, so with Widgets only your lights stayed on the last colour. Xenon now reads the cover itself in the background, and the lights change with every new song and go back to normal when the music stops.

  • Store widgets' Deck keys work with Widgets only

    A Deck key, or its keyboard shortcut, that runs a Store widget's own action used to wait three seconds and fail when no dashboard was open, and webhooks for that widget were lost. With Widgets only, Xenon now runs the widget's background part on its own, only while you have allowed one of its Deck actions, so the key answers at once and its lit state follows the widget. Nothing is added when no widget needs it.

  • Performance Mode works with Widgets only

    With no dashboard open, Performance Mode did nothing: no suggestion when a game started, and a session started earlier kept the High performance power plan on after the game closed. It now runs in the background. The suggestion appears as a card at the top right of your screen with Optimize and Don't ask again, automatic mode applies and restores by itself, and a short card says what changed. You can also ask Bit to optimize the PC. Closing apps stays a choice you make on the dashboard. Nothing runs while Performance Mode is off.

  • Performance Mode always ends its automatic sessions

    If you changed a Performance Mode setting while it was optimizing a game automatically, or the dashboard reloaded meanwhile, the session could stay on after the game ended, keeping animations paused and the power plan switched. It now ends a short while after the game, as it should. The suggestion also goes away as soon as you change these settings, instead of staying on screen until it times out.

  • Laptop battery and power mode, on every system

    On a laptop the Xenon menu now shows the battery under Now (percent, charging or the time left, in orange at 20% or less), and the Batteries tile and widgets get the laptop's own pack on a Mac and on Linux too, not only on Windows. Where the system lets an app change it, the menu also has the power mode (Saver, Balanced, Performance), and so does a new Deck key, Power mode, which can pick one or step to the next. You can ask Bit "how much battery is left?" or "switch to battery saver". On Windows the mode exists only on the Balanced power plan, so with another plan the key and the menu row do not appear and Bit says why. On Linux the mode needs power-profiles-daemon. On a Mac Xenon reads the battery and Low Power Mode but does not change it: macOS changes it only in System Settings, Battery. Fans, TDP and the maker's own power settings stay out on purpose.

  • The Xenon menu with a controller, and bigger targets on touch screens

    On a handheld such as the ROG Ally or the Legion Go, or with any controller on a PC, hold the two small buttons in the middle together for a moment (View and Menu on an Xbox-style controller, Create and Options on a PlayStation one) and the Xenon menu opens over your game. In the menu, the D-pad or the left stick moves between the buttons, A presses, B closes, and LB and RB change section; B also stops a shortcut that is waiting for keys. This works with Xbox-style and PlayStation controllers (DualShock 4, DualSense) on Windows, with any controller on Linux, and on a Mac as a Beta. To turn the hold off, use Open with a controller in the menu's Shortcuts and macros section, or ask Bit. On a touch screen the menu's buttons are now 48 pixels tall. The switches take presses from a larger area around them, on every screen. In SteamOS Game Mode no window can open over the game, so there the menu opens from the desktop or from the phone.

  • Build your own widgets with Claude Code or Codex

    If you write widgets with a coding assistant, connect it in Settings → Widgets & sharing → Build widgets with Claude Code or Codex (one button each), or add the xenon-mcp server to any other MCP client. The assistant can then read the Widget SDK, write a starter, install the widget and show it on your dashboard, read the errors it hits while it runs and look at a picture of its tile, then fix it, without you copying files around. The first time, the dashboard asks whether to allow it, and the connected tools are listed in that card with a Remove button. It never approves a widget's permissions for you, only touches widgets you made, and works only from the PC running Xenon. Picture of the tile: not on Linux under Wayland.

  • Bit plays a channel, a video or a page in its tile

    Ask "put on ibai's stream", "play this video" with a YouTube link, or "open ilmeteo.it in the browser tile", and it plays in the Twitch, YouTube or Browser tile, on the dashboard or on a widget on your screen, whichever has that tile; if more than one screen has it, only the one you are looking at plays it. Describe it instead ("a Minecraft stream", "lofi music") and the first live channel or video that fits plays, when your Twitch or YouTube account is connected in Settings. If no open screen has that tile, Bit says so and offers to add it. The Browser tile never opens this PC or your home network.

  • Bit works on the tiles you already have

    Bit can now show a dashboard page by its name ("show the Work page") or the next and previous one; pause, resume, restart or stop a timer or a stopwatch; change a task (its text, priority or how often it repeats) and move, rename or change a calendar event, with Undo; and work on one note among several: write a new note, add a line to the end of one ("add eggs to the shopping note"), replace it, pin it, open it or delete it. When the words fit more than one task, event or note, Bit asks which one instead of guessing.

  • Copy a capture into your own folders

    Ask Bit "save the last 42 seconds on the Desktop", or use the new Deck key "Copy to a folder" in the Capture group: the newest screenshot or video (or the one you name) is copied to the Desktop, Downloads, Documents, Pictures or Videos, and stays in the gallery too. If Instant Replay keeps less than you asked for, the clip has what it keeps and Bit tells you, and offers to keep more next time.

  • Voice Live can use your services

    In a live voice chat, Bit can now control Spotify, Home Assistant, Discord, OBS, Twitch, YouTube live broadcasts and Streamer.bot the same way it does in the written chat, when they are connected.

  • Bit changes your favourites

    Ask "add Tesla to my stocks", "follow Juventus", "add the Serie A" or "follow the news about AI", and Bit adds it the way the tile's own search would: a stock or a team by name, a news source by name, or otherwise a topic made of your words. It can also remove one ("take Napoli off") or say what you follow; when the words fit more than one, it asks which.

  • Do not disturb from Bit or a Deck key

    Ask Bit "do not disturb" or "mute the notification sounds", or add the new "Do not disturb" key (System group): it holds routine pop-ups back always, only during games and full-screen scenes, or never, the same choices as Settings, Notifications. Bit can also turn the pop-ups, their sound or every notification on and off. Errors, warnings, reminders and finished timers always come through.

  • Bit changes more of your settings

    Ask Bit to turn the song lyrics or their translation on or off, show the sound wave under the song, switch CPU and GPU temperatures to Celsius or Fahrenheit, change how the clock writes the date, turn the loading logo or the idle pause of animations on or off, or open the Ambient scene by itself after 1 to 30 minutes. Ask "what are my settings" and Bit reads them back. Open dashboards update right away.

  • Deck keys work in the Virtual Deck window and on screen widgets

    A Deck with a background picture or gradient showed nothing there. Ask Bit keys now reach the open dashboard, or Bit on the screen when you use widgets only, and say so when there is none. The Mixer key in the Virtual Deck window now lists the apps playing sound, and a key that fails there tells you why.

  • Windows a widget opens work on your screen too

    A calendar day, the Deck profile list, a smart home device, the disk advisor or a UniFi camera opened from a widget on your screen stayed invisible and could not be clicked. They now open on top, in your language, and close the usual way.

  • Choices made in a widget on your screen are kept

    A Discord favourite, the ChatGPT model, a lyrics option or a Notifications switch changed in a widget on your screen went back as before at the next reload. They are now saved like on the dashboard.

  • Set up buttons work in a widget on your screen

    The "Connect in Settings" button of Discord, Spotify, Twitch, YouTube, Streamer.bot, smart home, UniFi, disk cleanup and lyrics, and the slideshow's "Add images", did nothing there. It now opens the dashboard on the right Settings page. On the dashboard, the disk tile's button no longer closes Settings when they are already open.

  • Weather details open from a widget on your screen

    Tapping the weather widget there now opens the same details as on the dashboard: current conditions, hours and days.

  • Night hours show a moon

    The hourly forecast picked sun or moon by the time now, so in the evening every clear hour up to the next morning showed a sun. Each hour now follows its own time, and forecast days always show their daytime icon.

  • Remote control and Claude widgets on your screen use the dark dropdown

    Their menus opened as the plain white system list there. Ctrl+Space inside a widget on your screen no longer opens a search you could not see; the shortcut set for search still opens the real one.

  • Ask Bit about your Vitals

    Say "how is my water?", "I just drank" or "I took a break" and Bit reads the meters or fills them for you, with the same streak and level a tap on the bar gives. You can also ask Bit to stay quiet for 30 minutes or for the rest of the day, or to turn its pet on or off.

  • Bit can do anything a Deck key does

    Ask Bit to mute a Wave Link or Voicemeeter channel, mute a source in OBS, run a Streamer.bot action, colour one lighting device, play a sound from your soundboard or launch a Steam game, and it runs it now, the same way a key would. Before anything that types or presses keys for you, runs a script, calls or messages someone, posts to your stream or chat, locks the PC or unlocks a door, Bit shows a card with exactly what will run, and nothing happens until you tap Run.

  • Bit builds more of your Deck, and picks your sensors

    When Bit makes a Deck it can now set keys that switch on and off, keys that act only while held or repeat while held, keys that ask before they run, and how a lit key looks. Ask Bit which sensor your CPU or GPU temperature or wattage comes from, and it lists the sensors this PC has and switches to the one you name, or back to Automatic.

  • Bit's AI roasts can run on Sparks, with a daily limit you set

    With Sparks as your AI, turning on AI-generated roasts now shows how many Sparks a day Bit may spend on them: none (his own lines, the default), 10, 25, 50 or 100. At the limit he goes back to his own lines until the next day, and the count holds across a restart. Claude Code and Codex still never spend your plan on roasts.

  • Deck keys for your Vitals

    The new key "Refill a vital" in the Vitals group marks one meter done (water, food, a stretch, an eye break, posture) or all of them, from the Deck or a hardware key. Any key can also show how full a meter is, or the emptiest one by name, under "Live value" in the key editor; the number turns amber when the meter runs low and red when it is empty.

  • Widgets can show your Vitals

    Widgets you make in the Xenon Maker, without code, can show each meter, the emptiest one, your level and your streak, and a button in the widget can fill a meter. Widget authors get the same through the new vitals stream and action in the Widget SDK.

  • See your desktop wallpaper behind the dashboard, Wallpaper Engine included

    In the Xenon app, on Windows, macOS and Linux, Settings, Background has a new switch, Show the desktop behind the panels. The app window becomes transparent, so whatever is on that screen's desktop shows behind the tiles: an animated Wallpaper Engine scene, a video wallpaper or the plain one. How much shows through is up to Panel opacity and Background dim, in Appearance. Xenon's own backgrounds (aurora, grid, static, animated or uploaded) stay saved and simply step aside, so they come back as they were when you turn it off, and nothing keeps playing out of sight in the meantime. The window can only be made transparent when it is created, so Xenon asks and restarts when you switch it on or off. Where a transparent window cannot be drawn, Xenon keeps it solid and Settings says why: on a Windows PC whose screen hangs off a different graphics card from the one drawing the dashboard it would come out blank (and if a screen change later moves the window onto the other card, the app restarts by itself so it is never left blank), and on Linux it needs a compositor, which a Wayland session always has and an X11 one may not. If Wallpaper Engine pauses its wallpaper while Xenon is full screen, add a rule for xenon-native.exe in Wallpaper Engine's Performance tab with the Keep running action. Asked for on Discord. The browser, the iCUE panel and the phone are unchanged.

  • Reply to a Discord DM from the Discord widget

    Every DM or mention in the widget's Notifications tab now has a Reply button: it brings Discord to the front on your PC with that conversation already open, so answering takes one tap and a few words. Xenon does not write the message itself, because Discord gives apps no way to send one (the only way round it would use your account's token, which Discord treats as a self bot and can ban you for). It works on Windows, macOS and Linux; if Discord was closed, Xenon starts it and opens the chat once it is up, and if the chat cannot be opened it says so instead of pretending. On a paired phone the button is not shown, since you answer in the Discord app in your hand. Asked for on Discord.

  • A Browser tile can show one page on its own and still be reloaded

    (#149). With the toolbar hidden, the tile used to keep a single button, Show toolbar. It now keeps a small group in the corner with Reload, Full screen and Show toolbar, so a local web interface or a dashboard can sit in a tile with nothing else around it, and the toolbar comes back only when you want to go somewhere else. The tile remembers this, as before.

  • See who is in a Discord voice channel at a glance

    In the Discord widget, everyone in your call and in the channels under the Channels tab now shows with their Discord avatar beside their name. The avatar gets Discord's green ring while that person speaks, and a red microphone or a red pair of headphones after the name says they muted or deafened themselves. Someone you turned down yourself still shows with their name struck through. The avatars come straight from Discord, so they are not saved anywhere, and when one cannot load, a clean circle with the first letter of the name takes its place. Speaking and muting update in place, so the pictures never blink while people talk. In a light theme the Channels tab's server headings and counts are readable again. Asked for on Discord.

  • An anonymous count of which features get used, and a switch for it

    Settings → General → Updates has a new switch, Count which features I use, anonymously. When it is on, once a day Xenon sends how many times each of its features ran and how many times it failed, and whether a supporter code is saved on this PC. Only the feature name and a number: no identifier, nothing you type or make, never the code itself. It helps decide what to improve first. It starts on for new installs only; if you already use Xenon it stays off until you turn it on. Turning it off deletes the counts waiting to be sent, and a phone paired with your PC cannot change it. What is counted, on the site, in Xenon Maker and in the app, is on the privacy page.

  • Bit's face in place of his name

    The heads of the chat panel and of the Chat tile now show Bit himself instead of the word. Screen readers still read his name.

  • Bit lives on the search bar

    The sparkle button and the chat icon were two ways to reach the same Bit, so they are one now: Bit himself sits on the bar, on the Search tile and in the search overlay. He listens while you type, gets an idea when nothing is found, waves when you reach for him and says hello when the bar opens. Press him, or Ctrl+B, and the bar turns into his chat, in the same window and in your theme, with what you had typed already in the field. The last row of the results, "Ask Bit", sends the phrase straight away. Bit can search your files from the chat, so the old AI search mode and its Ctrl+I are gone. Paste a picture or a document straight into the bar, or attach one with the paperclip. The chat stays open while you go to another app to copy something: press the search shortcut to come back to it. Esc returns to the bar and a second Esc closes it. The rules are those of Bit's chat everywhere else: the same assistant, the same Sparks and the same limits. The window stays out of screen captures, so when you ask Bit to look at your screen it sees your screen and not the chat.

  • Your widgets in the Xenon menu

    A new row in Widgets: Open lists everything you created or installed, with update, export and remove, and Import takes a code, a link or the file saved by the Maker.

  • On an app is easy to pick, and stays out of the way

    In the Xenon menu, On an app lists your open apps with their own logo, stays pressed while the list is open, and then shows the app you chose. The same logos appear when you pick an app for When it shows. A widget in a top corner now sits under the strip of the app's window, so minimize, maximize and close stay within reach. Its screen changes the corner and the size, also while the app is closed, and moving it to another app keeps both. Bit does it too: "move the notes to the bottom left of Excel".

  • Performance Mode keeps busy apps out of the game's way

    If the processor stays near its limit during a game in a session, the heaviest other apps move to a few cores of their own and the game keeps the rest. On a stand-in game beside an app filling all 16 threads of our test PC, late frames went from about 60% to under 4% on Windows, and from 99% to 0.1% on Linux in a test container on the same PC. While the processor has room nothing moves, and nothing changes. The apps go back when the game or the session ends, even after a crash. The game, what it started, its launcher, Xenon, the system, background services, voice, streaming, meeting and overlay apps are never touched, nor is anything the game, Xenon or a voice, streaming, meeting or overlay app opened. A page an app shows through a web engine many apps share (WebView2, WebKit) moves and comes back with that app, never on its own. An app you bring to the front goes back at once with everything it opened, and stays out until the session ends. It is on by default inside Performance Mode, with its own switch in the sheet and in Settings, on Windows, macOS and Linux (Beta). Games played in a session are marked in your game history, so you can ask Bit whether it helped.

Improvements

  • The Mac helper updates with the app

    On a Mac, the small helper behind the app switcher, the search shortcut, file search and the Trash only moved to a new version when you ran the setup again. Now Xenon updates it by itself after an app update, when the app needs a newer one, and only with the file checked against the signed release. It is replaced only when it is too old, so macOS does not ask again for the Accessibility permission at every update.

  • A new logo: Bit

    The X is gone. The app icon, the taskbar and tray, the installer, the website, emails and the iCUE widget now show Bit, the small pixel robot, next to the name xenon.

  • Widgets know their limits from the start

    A community widget used to find out how much it could download only by trying a request first. Now Xenon tells it at start (init.limits in the Widget SDK): the size of an answer (4 MB), of a request, how often it may ask, its timeout, and how much it may store. An answer refused for being too large also says which size fits. Widgets made with Xenon Maker use this to read several websites one after the other instead of having some refused for a minute.

  • Less memory with the Minimal clock

    The tiles under the floating clock are cut around it with a shape that used to reach about 10,000 pixels down, far past the tile. On a glass tile the browser kept a 36 MB image of that whole shape, often several at once. The cut now ends just under the tile, which saves up to about 180 MB of graphics memory with no change to how it looks.

  • Each window loads only your language

    The dashboard, the search window (Alt+Space) and the Deck popup used to load the app's text in all eleven languages: 5.2 MB of text read at every start. Now they load your language and English only, about 0.8 MB, and each window keeps roughly half the script memory it used to. The other languages arrive the first time you search Settings or the widget list, so a word in any language still finds what you are looking for, and switching language in Settings fetches the new one in a moment, with no reload of the dashboard.

  • The Mac app is notarized by Apple

    From 5.0 Xenon for macOS is signed with an Apple Developer ID and checked by Apple, so it opens like any app downloaded from the internet: macOS asks once, you click Open, and there is no more trip to Privacy & Security for Open Anyway. Because the signature changes, macOS may ask once more for the permissions you had given Xenon (Full Disk Access, Accessibility, Screen Recording and the others): give them again once and they hold from then on.

  • Node.js on a Mac and on Linux

    Xenon still runs on Node.js 18 and 20, but those no longer get security fixes: the setup now says so and asks you to update to Node.js 22 or newer, and the log names the way to do it on your system (Homebrew on a Mac, your package manager on Linux) instead of a Windows command.

  • Bit adds keys to the Deck you already have

    Asked for a new key, Bit used to say it could only make a whole new profile. Now it puts the key in the first free spot of the profile in use (a new page when that one is full), and it can make a key with a single face, such as one that saves a replay. Its keys use the Deck's own drawn icons, which now include replay, screenshot, timelapse and picture, instead of an emoji that clashed with the rest. Its answer buttons also show as buttons when it writes them on one line, and it explains things in plain words instead of internal names.

  • A Deck key can keep one face

    A key whose action has a state of its own, like saving an Instant Replay, used to light up by itself and show an off and an on look. Under the preview, "Keep one look" now leaves a single face (the same switch is in the State tab, "Lights up on its own, following..."); "Back to off and on" brings the two faces back.

  • Screen tools have their own group in the Deck

    When you pick what a key does, the colour picker, the ruler, drawing on the screen, pinning, covering private data and copying text from the screen are now under Screen tools. Capture keeps what records the screen: screenshots, video, Instant Replay, timelapse and the gallery.

  • The Codex widget says what is happening

    Each session and conversation now says Working or Waiting for you in a word, instead of a coloured dot. The Usage tab shows a chart with today in colour and the numbers beside the days. When Codex is not installed or you are signed out, the tabs go away and only the next step stays.

  • Codex and Claude Code decisions always fit

    On a short widget a waiting decision takes the whole widget, with its keys beside it on a wide one, so Allow and Deny are never cut off. When decisions would stack, you see one at a time and how many are left.

  • A calmer Layout mode

    The Widget style window no longer dims the screen: it moves away from the widget you are dressing, rings it, and hides the edit handles until you close it. It keeps one height while you change tab, the tabs stay on one line, and Esc closes it before it leaves Layout mode. The layout bar now sits at the bottom of the screen and can still be dragged. On Liquid Glass the window, the bar and the page keys are the same glass as the rest of Xenon.

  • Tab groups read as titles

    On Liquid Glass, widgets that share a tile as tabs now show their names as the tile's titles: the open one bright and a little heavier, the others dimmer, lined up with what is under them. The strip of tabs that sat over the widget's own tabs looked like two rows of tabs and left most of the row empty; it is gone. A group you painted in your own colours in Widget style keeps its strip. System's first view is now called Overview, so a System tile in a group no longer says System twice.

  • Volume and Microphone are a mixer

    On Liquid Glass, the Volume and Microphone tabs of the System tile, and the Audio and Microphone widgets they become when you take them out of it, show every sound as a channel: its level, a fader wide enough for a finger, its name and its mute key. When there is room for all of them they stand side by side, as on a mixing desk; on a phone, a short tile or with many apps open they lie down as wide bars, so nothing has to be scrolled sideways. The level is the fill itself, with no handle to aim for. The Microphone tab and widget have one big key that says whether the mic is on and which one it is, and their level is now called Input volume, which is what it sets. Its level and apps also stay current while the tab is open: before, they kept the first reading. App names no longer end in .exe. The other looks are unchanged.

  • History groups its charts by unit

    The History tab of the System tile now shows one chart for temperatures, one for load and, when your PC reports watts, one for power, each with its own scale and the hours or days along the bottom. Point at a chart, tap it or use the arrow keys to read the exact values at any point. Temperatures use the unit you chose for hardware, Celsius or Fahrenheit. While History is open, its 24h, 7d and 30d buttons sit in the tab bar where Optimize was; Optimize now shows only on Overview. Screen time keeps its own card with your most used apps, games marked by a controller icon, and on a large enough tile everything fits without scrolling. The Energy widget's power history uses the same charts.

  • The Playback widget, redone

    On Liquid Glass the cover comes first and largest, play and pause sit on the one filled key in the cover's colour, and the other keys are plain symbols. When the widget has room it shows how far into the song you are, with the time at both ends: tap or drag the line to jump, and if the player cannot jump, Xenon says so. On a wide tile the cover starts right under the tabs, as large as the tile allows, with the keys level with its bottom, and the waveform keeps its strip below. The app's volume is the mixer's fader, with no handle, and Spotify's keys and lists follow the same look. With nothing playing, or a song that has no cover, the cover is a plain square with a note instead of the green bars.

  • Twitch, YouTube, OBS, Discord and Streamer.bot, redone

    On Liquid Glass the seven streaming tiles now look like the Playback widget. What you look for comes first: the picture, the viewer count on YouTube Live, and the people in a Discord call, who on a tall tile are large faces with their names under them, as in Discord. Live, Recording and the voice channel are words in their colour, in every language, with no badge or dot. Going live is the one filled key, in the service's colour; once you are live, ending it is a red word on a plain key. Keys that are only a symbol have no plate, a text field has its own send key that lights up when there is something to send, and tabs are plain words, the open one naming the tile. The OBS and Discord volumes and the YouTube progress line have no handle: the level is the fill. On the Xeneon Edge, OBS shows its preview large on the left with the keys and scenes beside it instead of a thin strip, Discord's two volumes share a line and Twitch's chat mode and ad break sit beside its keys, so nothing has to scroll and the chat keeps more room. On a phone, YouTube's keys stay on one row. Discord's volumes no longer start with "Discord:". Streamer.bot's events read as a list, the kind a symbol in its colour and the amount in words, and each global is its name and a bright value. A tile that still needs your account shows one key in its middle that opens Settings, and OBS, until it is set up or found on this PC, dims its keys instead of offering Go live. The other looks are unchanged.

  • File transfer, redone

    On Liquid Glass the File transfer tile now reads like the Send to PC screen on the phone: each file is a line with a larger name, its size, age and where it came from under it, and bigger keys. The dashed box shows only while you drag a file over the tile: an empty tile has its two keys in the middle, and once there are files they wait at the foot. "How it works" takes the place of the list instead of covering it. The other looks are unchanged.

  • Chat names read on a light theme

    The colour a viewer picks for their name is made for Twitch's dark chat, so yellow or light green names were hard to read on a light theme. They keep their colour, only darker, on every look. YouTube Live's owner, moderator and member names take darker shades there too.

  • See-through widgets stay readable with blur off

    On a low-power graphics chip, or with transparency turned off on your system, a thin glass panel turns thicker instead of leaving the words over the bare wallpaper.

  • A new Store

    It opens at full screen, with every section in a list on the left: Discover, Widgets, Packs, Themes, Backgrounds, Scenes and Deck profiles, then Installed and Sparks. A card is now just a picture and a name, and one tap opens a page that keeps the list beside it and fits a low screen such as the Xeneon Edge. Supporter packs come first as large posters in their own colours, with the price beside them, and Sparks come right after with what each pack costs. Shelves no longer repeat what is already under Just added, and they start with what people install most. A locked item says its price next to the key. When a search finds nothing, Bit offers to build it and writes your words in the chat without sending them. If the catalog cannot be reached, the Store says so and offers to try again.

  • You see when something from the Store has an update

    Bit tells you in its corner card: the name of the item, or how many have one, with a key, Open Installed, that takes you to the Store's Installed tab. There each row says under its name what it waits on, a new version or the permissions it needs to run, and one green key shows the next thing to do: Update all, or the first row waiting on you. It replaces the small notice that came and went once a day. A Store widget that updates by itself is given three days to do it, so you only hear about the ones waiting for you, such as an update that asks for a new permission, and the notice for those now opens Installed too. Bit tells you about an update once: what you already read about is not repeated. In the Xenon menu the Store shows how many updates are waiting and opens Installed, and on a phone the settings button shows the same count as on the PC.

  • Settings at full screen

    Settings now fill the window like the Store: every page in one list on the left, one calm column on the right, the same look under every theme, on the Xeneon Edge, in the window of the Xenon menu and on a phone. Every page is built the same way: the name on the left, a short line under it when it helps, the control on the right. What you change rarely sits in a closed row you open with a tap. An option that only works with a switch on now disappears while that switch is off, and a step this PC cannot do stays dimmed and says why. Repeated titles, preview strips, coloured boxes, status dots and small tags are gone, and a green key on a page is the next thing to do.

  • French, Russian and Portuguese speak to you one way

    French and Russian mixed the polite and the familiar form, sometimes in the same window; they now use vous and вы throughout (the lines you say to Bit, such as a suggested question, keep tu, as French speaks to an assistant). Portuguese mixed Brazil and Portugal, with você and tela next to tu and ecrã; it is now Portugal's Portuguese everywhere, with tu, ecrã, telemóvel, ficheiro and Definições. Searching in Settings still finds a setting by either country's word.

  • One word for supporter in each language

    Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Korean and Russian used two to four different words for the same thing, on the same buttons. Each now uses one, as on the site's menu where there is one.

  • Settings pages have clearer names and places

    The assistant's page is called Bit and sits higher in the list, the guardian's meters are Vitals, Background holds your own media first and the animated backgrounds after it, and Claude Code and Codex share one page. A new About page holds the version, the update check, Discord, GitHub, Report a bug, the tutorial, restart and reset. Calendar settings moved from General to Calendar, the preview of the Edge to Display, the position and test of notifications to Notifications, and General now reads Dashboard, This PC, Updates and news, Privacy, Backup. In Appearance, Mode and Accent sit with Themes, and everything you can fine-tune sits under Personalize. A link from a tile now scrolls the list to the page it opens.

  • Windows that ask you something are one family

    On the Liquid look the page behind blurs and the window sits on it as glass. The title says what is going on, the main key is on the right with the safe one beside it, Esc closes only the window on top, Tab stays inside and the keyboard goes back where it was. The screensaver and promo cards wait while one is open.

  • Bit's cards sit under the top bar

    A message from Xenon, a rating question and the performance suggestion appear at the top centre, below the bar, and no longer cover the clock. With no bar folded, Bit waits in the corner of the screen. Full-screen messages moved from yellow to lavender, so Bit stands out on them.

  • Xenon can talk to supporters or to everyone else

    A message from the Store can now be aimed at one group or the other. Versions before 5.0.0 do not show these messages.

  • Calmer update windows

    The update window, its notes and the window after a failed update share one look, and the manual download sits with the quiet keys. On a phone Later and Download stay side by side.

  • The December note and the Discord card match the rest

    The note lost its pink, heart and glow and uses your theme's main key.

  • Performance suggestion, clearer

    It is a card at the top, with Ignore as a real key. The window that follows has Bit at the top, memory in plain words and no tags, and the result is an ordinary notification with the memory freed on its own line.

  • Share and import windows, one main key each

    The extras are a list, Cancel sits beside a review, and a key that deletes is a red word on Liquid.

  • The Weather window, redone

    It uses the same parts as the tile and adds sunrise and sunset. A wrong city gets an Open settings key, and it has a proper loading state.

  • The day window reads the way you plan

    The time comes first, keys sit on the right, Esc closes it and Enter saves. The time picker works from the keyboard: it opens on the hour, Tab goes to the minutes, the arrow keys change them and Enter closes it.

  • Bit's confirm cards use plain names

    A Deck action reads as words, not code. A command for your PC stays word for word on purpose, so you can see what will run.

  • Incoming calls

    Decline is on the left and Answer on the right, and Esc dismisses the call.

  • The device picker and the colour picker

    The device list is centred, with a check mark on the one in use and a line when there is nothing to pick. The colour picker no longer closes after each drag, and its hue strip and shade square now work from the keyboard: Tab to them, then the arrow keys, with Shift for bigger steps.

  • Disk analysis

    Xenon Storage Advisor is now Disk analysis: one list that opens row by row instead of a report in small print, with an Ask Bit key. The same categories no longer appear twice, and the confirm panel on the tile has Cancel on the left and the main key on the right.

  • The Gallery opens at full screen

    It has the same list on the left as the Store, with your games and how many captures each holds, and the space used at the foot. Pictures and videos open in a dark room on every look, Space plays or pauses, and Esc goes back one step at a time.

  • Game Companion, tidier

    The page behind blurs, Analyze is the one main key with its price beside it, and a long answer scrolls with the keys on screen. Over a game the price now shows too, and the card still never takes the keyboard from the game.

  • One request window for Codex and Claude Code

    It says what happens if nobody answers, counts several requests, and a plan reads as text instead of raw markdown. Esc answers as the terminal would: it denies a Claude Code request and goes back to Codex for Codex.

  • The Xenon menu looks like Settings

    It has the same list on the left and the same page, and looks the same under every theme. Green is only for what is on and for the one main key. Long names wrap instead of being cut.

  • The widget questions are the same sheet

    Permissions, copying to the clipboard, opening a site and pairing a coding tool share one look, and they now work on widgets on your screen and on scenes too.

  • Add widget is a gallery

    Each widget has a real picture and one line that says what it does, and Store widgets show their Store picture. One Esc closes only the panel on top.

  • The four Deck windows are one family

    The key editor, Deck appearance, Smart Profiles and the mixer share one plate and one look on every theme. The editor has Esc and keeps Tab inside, and on a phone on its side the list on the left stays. Pressing outside the editor or Smart Profiles closes them only if nothing changed.

  • Send to PC

    The keys sit at the foot with Photos and videos as the main one, rows are larger, and How it works takes the whole sheet instead of a small box. On a phone on its side, the list and the notes scroll together. On a phone you can also pull the sheet down by its title to close it, as with the phone's own sheets.

  • The cookie box on the site

    It sits at the page's left edge on computers and lines up with the page on phones. Reject still comes first, and both keys are the same size.

  • Services in Settings show what you can use

    Smart Home, Cameras, Spotify, Streaming, Lighting, Phone and Remote Control give each service its own section, keep How to connect out of the way once you are set up, and show what needs a connection only after it is connected. Claude Code and Codex, Performance, Capture and Widgets & sharing follow the same rows: in Performance the lists of activities, apps and readings are closed rows, and each context profile says what it switches to.

  • Search in Settings finds more

    It now finds sections, closed rows and keys such as Export or Delete games, shows the place of each result, and marks the row it takes you to. A result behind a switch that is off takes you to that switch, so you always land on something you can see.

  • No supporter pitch for supporters

    With a saved supporter code, the Store no longer shows the window that explains the membership: every link to it goes straight to the Supporters list. Everyone else gets a new window with real packs, the price and what is included.

  • A new install asks one question

    Xenon used to open with two dialogs in a row, with a Discord card and a stock alert on top of them. Now one window shows your real screens and what each one will hold, with a recommended answer already selected, and your choice puts the dashboard on the screen you tapped and three first widgets on your desktop. If you update, nothing is asked and nothing moves.

  • The first question looks like the rest of Xenon

    It now opens as glass over the new wallpaper, with your real screens drawn in it, and it melts into your dashboard when you answer. On a low-power graphics chip, or with animations off in the system, it simply closes.

  • Xenon no longer waits for Google to appear

    The fonts of the Retro and Comic looks held back the first frame until Google answered, so on a network that blocks Google the screen stayed black until the connection gave up. Now Xenon shows right away, and those looks use their fallback font until the real ones arrive.

  • Bit stays with you while Xenon starts

    On a first start Bit no longer disappears just before the first question, and the pictures in the question fade in instead of popping.

  • Your first day is yours

    News and drops from Xenon start the day after you install it, so nothing asks for your attention while you set up.

  • The tour waits until you want it

    It no longer starts by itself. Bit offers it in the empty chat, and the side buttons show themselves for a moment after the first question. It is also shorter: four stops, Bit, Search, the layout and Settings, where the last one says where to take it again. The welcome and goodbye cards are gone.

  • Less talking on the first day

    The Discord card waits for your second day of use, the hint about the swipe gesture comes at your first touch and only on a touch screen, and stock alerts start once you use stocks: with the ticker on, the tile on a screen, or a list of your own. If you kept the default list with no tile and no ticker, those alerts stop.

  • A new Deck looks like the rest of your dashboard

    A Deck you have not set up yet starts on the Theme base, the tile of your look, instead of the dark metal body. A Deck you already made keeps its base, and you can change it in Deck appearance.

  • Network draws a graph too

    The Network card in the System tile now shows a graph of your download speed, like CPU, GPU and the other cards, in place of the name of the network card.

  • An official Xenon drop now installs like one

    In the Store, a drop published by Xenon opens as an install, with an Install button and a line saying it comes from Xenon, instead of the Import preset window and its warning about code written by others. Community entries and codes shared by people keep that warning, and the review and the permissions you approve are the same for everyone.

  • Clearer words about the pass, the trial and Sparks
